research_in_progress.name: Southern Windcut diplomacy and White-Reed route
research_in_progress.stage: Year14 Day19 initial Windcut people contacted politely; two consented visits, no permanent accord; White-Reed Point marked offshore only, sandbar needs more observations.

research_in_progress.name: Practical cross-community Shore Words and interpretive teaching
research_in_progress.stage: Year14 Day342: 67 meanings and three short repeatable trade/safety utterances verified with consenting partners; four spoken forms unresolved; grammar not fully shared.

research_in_progress.name: Windcut and Taluma tidal-lashing durability comparison
research_in_progress.stage: Two consented binding methods installed for observation by local hosts; await a full tidal cycle before claiming improvement or negotiating dependable repeat exchange.

research_in_progress.name: Interpretation of conditions, exceptions and disagreements
research_in_progress.stage: Year15 Day249: 112 repeatedly verified Shore Words meanings; free-versus-barter distinction and a conditional monitoring request demonstrated with Windcut partners in one context, wider conversational grammar still unproven.

research_in_progress.name: Windcut season-long fishing stake abrasion and repair comparison
research_in_progress.stage: Year15 Day249: four free reinforced replacement sets delivered to affected Windcut fishers. Limited grit/tide handling observed, full storm-season durability unverified. Vara and local users retain monitoring authority.

research_in_progress.name: Wet-dry abrasion comparisons and field validation of braided cordage
research_in_progress.stage: Year15 Day307: controlled Taluma tests compare two-ply and braided lashings with revised knot patterns. Early braided samples loosened; promising retests remain preliminary. Await willing Windcut host field reports, and do not claim sea-season durability or commercial product superiority.

buildings_and_infrastructure: Ten mixed reed-and-hide shelters, capacity 55
Communal hearth
Five fish drying frames
One spring catchment lined with stones
Temporary freshwater jars
Two six-person weatherproof reed-and-pole shelters on rooted upper dune bench, provisioned by carried water (12 housed on bench; not a self-sufficient outpost)

Small raised stone-and-reed upstream draw point and drainage groove separating upper seep collection from the tidally affected lower catchment; covered woven holding jars on a marked carry route (a partial, provisional water safeguard)

Storm reinforcement: tightened lashings and strengthened entrances for both occupied upper-dune shelters; three original shelter roofs patched/reinforced; minor seam leak from Day 31 squall repaired. Shallow rainwater drainage channels refreshed. No extra housing capacity.
Maintained shallow drainage channels and the raised spring draw point during Days 36-45; no new structures, no change in housing capacity.
One experimental stone-and-clay draft-baffled hearth (not yet established to lower community fuel needs)
Two provisional timber-carrying frames and a partially cleared marked corridor to the northwest wooded swale (not an all-weather trail)
Council-supervised teaching rota at existing workspaces, no new schoolhouse; single experimental baffle hearth tested, no rollout

Two additional small prototype stone-and-earth wind-baffled cooking hearths (three prototypes total). One demonstrated poor draft in damp weather; none have been adopted as a general fuel-efficiency standard.
Two hand-sized test sowing patches with locally gathered wild grass seed near the settlement away from the protected drinking-water seep; research trial, not a producing field.

Day 105: Three existing prototype hearths retested and one smoke outlet adjusted with gathered local clay-rich silt; no new hearth, significant stone expenditure, or population-wide fuel efficiency credit.

Day 115: Planned only, an optional third 6-person high-dune shelter site beside existing two shelters; no structure built, housing capacity still 67. Proposed material cost 6 poles/12 cured reeds/1 stone load/1 cordage coil. Maintain repairs reserve before starting.

Day 135: one sheltered, raised reed-and-pole canopy over the most vulnerable fish-drying frames; two sound poles, three cured reed bundles and one cordage coil consumed. Performance in severe storms not yet proven.

Day 135: one reinforced timber-carrying frame for short-relay hauling; one straight pole and one cordage coil consumed. A limited trial brought one settlement fuel-day-equivalent (included in fuel ledger). No all-season road or permanent inland harvesting operation.
Day 135: prospective third six-person high-dune house site marked and leveled by hand without occupying new land or erecting a completed shelter; current capacity remains 67.

Day 160: Third six-person weatherproof reed-and-pole shelter completed on established high-dune site (capacity now 73 total, 67 occupied), after 3 previously damp reed bundles cured and 3 straight poles gathered; water supply at current weather provisionally supports an extra 6 but drought safety unknown. One additional carrier will be allocated when needed. Village retains 4-pole, 8 cured-reed, 1 stone and 1 cordage emergency reserve.

Days 188-207: wind-shaken raised cover over fish-drying rack repaired using one straight pole and one cured reed bundle; reduced future weather exposure but one food-day spoiled before repair. No new dwelling construction; housing remains 73 total.

Day 263: two existing cooking-hearth prototypes are in supervised daily use with basic observed smoke safety; one problem prototype remains unsuitable for indoor use. Hearths were not newly built and no stone expended; measured fuel benefit recorded as 1 settlement-fuel-day equivalent across the last nine days.

Days 225-263: small repairs to drying cover and older shelter roof consumed one straight pole and two cured reed bundles; no housing capacity added or subtracted. Existing six-place house has two people from the previous 67-person population forming a separate household, so 73 total places and 67 occupied remain unchanged.

Year 2 Day 74: simple sheltered shelf and reed windscreen built in existing work area for drying local clay prototypes; 1 wood pole and 2 reed bundles used, replenished through local gathering; no new dwelling or kiln constructed.

Year 2 Day 94: Dedicated open-sided pottery drying shelter and an adjacent clay-lined outdoor pit-firing area constructed on previously used Taluma work land, under Vessa and Arel. Workshop costs 2 straight poles, 4 seasoned reed bundles, 1 cordage coil, locally gathered clay; the single reserve stone load is not used. Space is deliberately ventilated and kept separated from family roofs. Nine small new vessels tried over the period; five survived firing, two held water overnight in testing, but no durable sealed bulk storage or large kiln exists.

Year 2 Days 88-103: Letha learned the principle of moving water around fish-weir stones through demonstrations by the Shellbend fishers on a loose pebble model at the margin of the cove. Their actual stone trap was not touched by Talumans; no joint fishery built, and no new fishing access or boundary rights accepted.
Year 2 Day 116: One infant, Nala, born to Rema and Jorin in their already occupied high-dune family home, safely assisted by Seli and two experienced caregivers. No increase in housing capacity.

Year 2 Days 125-156: Taluma built and revised a small removable tidal stone-and-woven-basket fish guide within its own lagoon, not at Shellbend. Initial high-tide washout required resetting the stone guide. The pilot is productive in normal tides but unproven against severe storms; no permanent fish-weir or fishing rights elsewhere were established.

Year 2 Day 148: Workshop drying shelves and a small reed shade screen improved slow clay curing, using 1 straight pole and 1 reed bundle; no kiln or large structure built. Six of eleven new low-fired pots survived; three held water overnight. Two days of extra firing fuel credited in the period.

Year 2 Day 196: two removable Taluma-lagoon tidal stone guides and woven creels now function in normal tides. One early new creel failed in a winter surge and was retethered; no permanent stone weir or Shellbend intrusion. Creels include a small-fish release practice being evaluated.

Year 2 Days 167-198: small existing Taluman-side headland clay and stone carrying route received stone markers, safe foothold clearance and lashings for portable carry frames. It is no fixed road and no new territory is claimed.
Year 2 Day 182: recurring Open Learning Days held using existing craft workspaces and Circle of Witnesses gatherings, not a separate school building.

Year 2 Day 239: Hall of Many Hands completed on Taluma’s existing sheltered dune village ground as an open-sided shared learning and exchange shelter with six poles, nine adequately cured reed bundles, one stone load and two cordage coils. Simple raised dry display surface and moveable mats; no closed public storage and no claim of fireproofing. Spent materials replenished partly via routine gathering (five poles, nine reeds, one stone load gathered, one cordage coil made); current stock ledger intact. First supervised learning gathering held Day 242 and voluntary guest demonstrations Day 244. Council assigns maintenance without repeat player instructions.

Year 2 Days 214-245: Corun observed a small second surface trickle in a sheltered western dune hollow, still on already-used Taluma land, after spring rain. Four checks over several weeks yielded small amounts of fresh-tasting water, but the trickle diminished after a dry interval. A small clay-lined trial collection hollow cracked and leaked. It is not certified drinkable, independent, or year-round reliable; the upper protected seep remains the sole proven daily supply.

Year 2 Days 254–274: Corun, Arel and a rotating crew constructed two modest rainwater collection trials on already-occupied Taluma ground: a stone-edged, reed-screened runoff basin below an existing roof and a shallow clay-sealed catchment near the western dunes. The latter cracked after partial drying and lost most stored water. The roof-fed basin retained rainwater for several days but collected leaf debris after the first storm; it is designated for mixing clay, rinsing tools and cleaning equipment, NOT for drinking, cooking, bathing wounds, infant use or other potable applications. Roof runoff diverted away from the protected freshwater seep; no verified independent drinking-water backup.

Year 2 Day 281: First annual Meeting of Many Hands held at the existing Hall of Many Hands after several weeks of voluntary invitations. Willing inland craft and Shellbend fisher guests attended open demonstrations and oral accounts, with ample freedom to leave. Food provided, no residential, trade, fishing, woodland, jurisdictional or binding rights negotiated. Council records intent to invite neighbors again around the same seasonal point next year, with no obligation on them to attend.

Year 2 Days 301-333: scouts marked a temporary safe return path to Western Gravel Run with small removable stone markers. This is not a built water channel, protected well, supply road, settled outpost or secured claim. Roof-runoff craft-water catchment remains nonpotable.

Year 2 Day 353: a small open-sided, removable trading shelter and marked exchange mats installed adjacent to the existing Hall of Many Hands on Taluman-occupied land, costing 2 straight poles and 2 cured reed bundles. This is a gathering area, not an occupied market town, marketplace monopoly, customs office, mint or bonded trade post.

Year 3 Day 4: Western Gravel Bench surveyed as a POSSIBLE future outpost site only. No buildings, water channels, fortified boundary, dwellings or territorial claim; Western Gravel Run is not a confirmed independent safe potable source.

Year 3 Day 18: trading area organized around one explicitly described level-fill reference reed basket, counting stones and visible freshness checks. Movable equipment, not currency, prices, tax, state standards or a new permanent building.

Year 3 Days 20-44: pottery workshop added improvised dry storage shelves and three fitted trial lids, with mixed firing results and no certified all-weather food preservation. Limited production while fuel constrained.

Year 3 Day 49: existing six-place spare shelter capacity used for three new residents; 71/73 occupied, two places free. No new house built or outpost founded; main spring water courier rotation adjusted for increased demand.
Year 3 Day 78: first additional four-place family shelter completed on already-settled high dune, with secure reed roof, wind lashings and safe cooking clearance; available housing capacity +4.

Year 3 Day 82: second additional four-place family shelter completed nearby; total housing capacity rises from 73 to 81. Construction materials spent 6 poles, 10 reed bundles and 2 coils for shelters; two repair poles and bundled reeds retained in stock after ordinary gathering.

Year 3 Days 63-89: upper freshwater spring received removable reed debris screen, raised clean-container rests and separated filled-water staging zone; worker rota cleans containers and assigns safe household carry. No well, pipe network, dam, independent supply or safe potability of rainwater established.
Year 3 Day 164: third Taluma-lagoon removable tidal fish guide and raised wind-screened fish-drying rack; one guide repaired after severe tide. No access to Shellbend fishing works.
Year 3 Day 151: Anet and Boran voluntarily established a shared household in existing Taluma housing, with the marriage recorded by the Circle of Witnesses; housing capacity unchanged.

Year 3 Days 178–202: Tama, Boran and Arel trialed a two-layer overlapping reed roof, wind-screened door edges and elevated sleeping mats on two occupied family shelters, consuming four reed bundles, one pole brace and one cordage coil from lawful stores. Open vent clearances and smoke pathways inspected; no new housing places created, no sealed smoky hearth accepted.

Year 3 Days 190–225: Nemi and Anet maintained protected fish drying surfaces and taught families how to sort moisture-exposed fish for re-drying rather than storing it wet. Food yield gains counted in 68 settlement-days of observed gathering/preservation; no farming harvest imagined.

Year 3 Day 211: the Council of the Shore reviewed a staged capacity sketch for 100 residents: at population 73 with capacity 81, at least nineteen additional housing places required; five four-person shelters would bring total capacity to 101, subject to material and water clearance. No five shelters built or population target declared achieved.

Year 3 Days 230-290: material supply earmarked, NOT CONSTRUCTED, for two possible four-place family houses: 8 poles, 14 reeds (some still curing), 2 stone loads, 2 cordage coils. Separate repairs stock 8 poles/11 reeds/3 stone/2 cordage remains accessible. Existing housing capacity stays 81.

Year 3 Days 272-286: one existing dwelling received a reversible raised woven resting platform, small outer stone runoff course and a detachable reed wall panel, incorporating separate Shellbend and inland shelter ideas without sealing smoke vents. Cost 1 pole/2 reeds/1 stone/1 cordage from current stocks; no new capacity.

Year 3 Days 252-282: improved covered spring staging/flow comparison, cost 1 wood pole and 2 reed bundles; improves safe collection hygiene and reduces some waste, but not independent source yield. 100-person water carrying capacity still unknown.

Year 3 Days 291-354: Vessa and Corun adapted the existing pottery workshop and raised spring draw area for eight small covered-clay storage tests. Of five fired intact, three initially held water, but one deteriorated visibly after several days; remaining two are strictly short-duration daily-refilled trial jugs. A stone platform used one local stone load and no permanent cistern or new potable source was built.

Year 3 Days 313-347: Boran and Tama strengthened one existing shelter with taught replaceable wall lashings and drainage repair, using 1 pole and 3 operational reed bundles. Existing housing capacity 81 unchanged, no new dwellings funded from protected earmarked future-family shelter materials.

Year 3 Day 355 through Year 4 Day 47: Arel, Tama, Boran and rotating adult building apprentices retrofitted four EXISTING homes in stages using unearmarked P3/R5/S2/C2. Reversible woven wall sections, raised sleeping areas and simple outside stone splash/drain courses were used. One roof-edge trench initially channeled stormwater back to a sleeping platform; repaired before being repeated elsewhere. Smoke outlets left open, no unsafe enclosed hearth, no additional capacity claimed. At least three retrofits stood up to ordinary autumn downpours; severe storm endurance not yet proven.

Year 4 Day 24: Hall of Many Hands assigns dedicated covered demonstration bays and mentorship time (no additional permanent building) for four adult skill paths: shelter, food/fish preservation, pottery/craft, water and measurement with cultivation lessons. Maro and Vessa maintain an oral record of completed observed practice, not a written credential.

Year 4 Days 57-101: Arel, Tama and Boran progressively improved THREE more EXISTING homes with dry elevated sleeping surfaces, replaceable reed panels, checked smoke gaps, graded drainage and roof-outlet protection. One new outlet initially sent runoff toward a walkway; corrected after a storm. Cost together with catchment trials P4/R8/S2/C3 unearmarked. No additional housing places; total capacity81.

Year 4 Days 63-104: two removable roof-to-lined-catchment rainwater trials were built on Taluma occupied land. First installation had uncovered leaking basin and dirty first-rainwater, so workers drained, cleaned and revised it. One covered lining now catches intermittent rain; 20 large jug-loads collected over three showers for only nonpotable washing, claywork and equipment cleaning. The potable spring remains separate and its actual water-output limit unchanged.

Year 4 Day89: Hall of Many Hands displays simple five-part construction testing reference panels and small marked clay strips for drainage direction/roof ventilation, while experienced mentors verify each apprentice’s practical inspection before they lead repairs.

Year 4 Days 76-107: Maro, Vessa, Corun and older learner Leni began a consistent nonphonetic pictographic/tally marking set on small drying clay tiles and wood strips. Examples preserve measurements of collected rain, clay vessels and dates; speech, personal names and fuller history remain oral. Low-fired tablets and copies reside at Hall; no alphabet or full written language.

Year4 Days120-169: Arel and Corun expanded roof-rainwater capture on existing Taluma village roofs with two additional removable channels and a stone-edged, clay-lined covered communal basin (capacity ~18 large jugs). Two of three roof feeds usable after storm regrading; third isolated following leaking/discolored stagnant water. Total 72 captured jug-loads across repeat rains, 54 used for nonpotable cleaning and clay work, 14 lost/discarded, four covered on Day175. No new drinking source, no housing-capacity gain, reserve stone/reed earmarks untouched.

Year4 Days125-173: Hall of Many Hands now has small stored clay/wood sign samples depicting person, household token, shelter, rain, water vessel, wet/full/dry/empty, inward/outward movement, and counted goods. Apprentice readers independently recognize some records without speaking to author; full stories, phonetic names and speech still belong to oral Circle of Witnesses.

Year4 Day167: existing Anet-Boran family shelter prepared using previously tested dry raised bedding and smoke-safe roof, without adding new housing places; Seli and care network welcomed baby Tavi. Family support supplied from four-day protected food provision and care mat stores, rotated/replenished without stock double counting.

Year4 Day210: Arel and Corun improved accessible runoff-first-flush bypass and cleaned two covered rainwater-basin inlets on existing Taluma roofs; a previously failed third gutter was patched and remains test-only pending storms. Rainwater reserved mainly for crafts/washing, with just small supervised batches heated for near-term emergency drinking experiments. Roof dirt and longstanding stagnation remain risks. No spring-source gain or new claimed land.

Year4 Day225: Taluma raised, covered archive shelving installed in the Hall of Many Hands from 2 poles, cured reeds, a stone plinth and cordage. Stone-backed dry bins separate fragile raw tablet records from nine fired benchmark tablets; five unfired records had been damaged by an unexpected leak before this improvement. No new housing places or independent building erected.

Year4 Days241-303: Corun and Iren modified heat-shock-resistant trial clay vessels using gradual warming and properly vented covers, with careful handling; no new boiling workshop or permanent potable reservoir. One failed small pot and one dirty-transfer trial rejected; existing spring remains drinking-water baseline.

active_projects.lead: Arel
active_projects.description: Original trial and two new stone-and-earth baffles: moderate wind performance, but one unit smoked in damp weather. More repeat trials, weatherproofing and material cost-benefit needed. Fuel-day consumption rate unchanged. Day 105: wet-silt adjustment and further paired cooking trials; scale-up would need material/health-cost assessment. Day 115: repeat winter trials on existing units, no new stone spending; use one unit outdoors only until smoke issue resolved. Next: quantify cooking share of total fuel, repair costs, ventilation and wind effects. Days 126-135: repeat matched cooking tests and ventilation/smoke observations. Two sheltered prototypes again used roughly 9-12% less wood in favorable conditions, but outside heating/cooking split remains unmeasured. Third tested outdoors only in crosswinds. No additional stones used or fuel saving credited to reserves. Day 263: two safety-cleared units now serve normal cooking under supervision. Recorded 1 actual settlement fuel-day equivalent saved during Days 255-263 from measured fuel consumption; third hearth is not used in living areas.

Days 126-135: Tovan tested a reinforced frame using 1 straight pole and 1 cordage coil, cleared short snags within the already explored route, returned one fuel-day in a limited relay included within nine fuel-days gathered. Muddy segments still slow workers; no claims made to strangers’ land.

Council aims to preserve emergency supplies (4 poles, 8 cured reed bundles, 1 stone load, 1 coil). Current stock 9 poles, 19 mixed-age reed bundles, 2 stone loads, 4 coils; at least 1 pole/1 dry reed and curing time still needed before considering construction under reserve policy. Carried-water reliability and seasonal wind also gates. No pregnancies or new residents assumed. Days 126-135: previous partly damp reeds finished curing; several cured reeds spent on sheltered drying-rack work; 3 newly cut reeds need curing. Quality tally 17 dry and 3 green. With planned house and emergency reserve together needing 10 poles and 20 cured reeds, materials remain short by 1 pole and 3 cured bundles. Preliminary spring carrying-flow test promising for six additional people in current conditions, but council withheld start until materials/rest/weather ready. Day 160: construction completed from authorized materials with repair reserve preserved; added six spare spaces, pending future household use and water monitoring.

known_peoples.identifier: Unidentified people of the inland stream
known_peoples.status: Year 2 Day 32: Two inland visitors willingly came to Taluma for a daylight, nonbinding craft exchange after repeated invitation gestures at the ochre cord. Vessa and Iren demonstrated fiberwork; an inland guest demonstrated clay tempering/forming. No treaty, new timber rights, renewed escorted harvesting, or player-unapproved crossing of the ochre boundary. Trust improves but language and social identity remain largely unknown. Year 2 Days 142-150: one inland clay worker accepted a separate voluntary invitation to join a daytime Taluma craft gathering and showed tempering techniques; left before dark, no crossing permission for Talumans or binding agreement. Year 2 Days 291-333: willing visitors demonstrated a limited, counted exchange with Taluma. Inspected goods and reciprocal assent were important. No general or binding barter agreement, currency, land rights, new crossings, fishing permission or guaranteed future attendance. Year 2 Days 353-Year 3 Day 2: invited visitors could trade voluntarily at Taluma; no obligation to return, right to reject damp or unsuitable goods respected. Their own land and installations remain unchanged. Year 3 Day 49: Voluntary nonbinding Taluma barter demonstrations used an optional matched reed-basket measure; each group still controls its own places. Three individual Shellbend-origin people chose to become Taluma residents without transferring any community rights. Year 3 Days 291-354: reciprocal craft apprenticeships proceeded by named short host-approved limited visits and separately invited guest teachers. Each permission was visit-specific and expired; no new crossing corridor, extractive rights, treaty or ownership established.
known_peoples.location: far bank of the stony inland stream beyond the wooded swale
known_peoples.known_facts: Two adults first sighted Day 81; on Day 92 two people met four Taluman visitors from opposite banks. One of the visitors had a red-ochre band on their wrist. A modest dried-fish gift was accepted; a small woven fiber loop was placed in return. Their identity, language, number, village, motives and claims remain unknown. Day 167: three adults emerged along the marked inland route to the vicinity of Taluma; one wore a similar red-ochre wrist band and displayed a woven loop. Identity as exactly the same prior pair is not confirmed. They laid a tied, closed bundle on the ground and waited beyond the first dwellings; its contents and purpose unknown. At the Day 167 boundary meeting, the visitors unwrapped two finely flaked dark stone pieces and a small ochre-marked cord loop, displaying them as apparent exchange goods. Tovan, Esha and Nemi received them outside the dwellings. Talumans offered drinking water and a modest serving of dried fish from normal daily allotments. One visitor touched the ochre band, pointed back along the inland path and repeated a short word sounding like "Aru"; its meaning is unknown. When Tovan gestured toward the wooded swale, the visitor lowered an open palm and spoke quickly; no reliable meaning can be assigned to the gesture. They departed peacefully before sunset. Day 224: Three Talumans (Esha, Tovan and Vessa) met two watchers outside the ochre cord. Repeated demonstration using a stick and a flat palm conveyed an apparent prohibition on crossing the marked route; a separate gesture pointed toward a path bending to the stream. No one passed the cord. The watchers appeared to recognize the prior ochre-woven exchange token. No word meanings or land boundaries were determined. Days 264-291: Esha delegated Tovan and Vessa to three peaceful no-crossing meetings at the cord, accompanying them to the final conversation. Over repeated pointing and counting demonstrations they distinguished fallen limbs from standing trees, and arranged four stones beside four modest timber pieces and four small fish baskets. An inland elder/representative indicated a narrow approach to fallen wood through an escorted passage, not unrestricted entry. It appeared to invite a four-visit wood-for-fish trial with guides, while rejecting live cutting or entry elsewhere. No shared language or clear measure of loads, duration or boundary ownership; the suggested terms are a cautious interpretation, NOT a concluded offer or agreement. Days 292-320: Under explicit, conditional player authorization, Esha, Tovan and Vessa returned on Day 295 and repeated an object demonstration: four stones/four visits; a single modest preserved-fish basket at each trip; fallen limbs only, live trees untouched; one route selected by the inland people; guided entries only. The inland representatives repeated and assented to the same arrangements, pointed out the corridor themselves and reconfirmed per visit. Taluma did not cross until this confirmation. Four escorted visits (Days 298, 305, 312, 319) yielded 3+2+2+2=9 Taluma settlement-days of deadwood, against 4 baskets containing a total of 2 settlement-days of preserved food. On the third visit, a Taluman worker reached toward a still-rooted branch and an inland guide stopped the action; the worker withdrew without cutting it. On the final visit, guides closed the path behind the party. The two peoples retain only rudimentary gestural understanding. No identified village, official name or sovereign ownership established, and no renewal rights conveyed. Days 321-362: Vessa and Tovan made three courteous daylight meetings outside the ochre cord. A putative word sounding like "aru" was repeated while someone pointed toward running water; whether it refers to water, river, a specific place or something else is still unproven. The parties can reliably indicate fish, water and fallen wood with shared object/pointing gestures, but not quantities for renewed trade or political terms. They displayed a small hard-fired-looking clay bowl across the cord, without passing it or teaching its manufacture; Taluma has not developed pottery. A modest one-food-day-equivalent total of hospitality/exchange food came from ordinary stores. No new timber pilot, treaty, crossing, or land claim. Year 2 Days 7-17: Taluma proposed hosting a peaceful craft demonstration using repeated gestures and a neutral basket/cord display at the boundary. Two inland participants voluntarily visited the coastal communal work area and were offered food. They watched Vessa and Iren splice and twist fiber, demonstrated mixing small crushed mineral/shell particles into a clay sample, and formed a small vessel by hand. They took their own vessel with them; the Taluman effort later cracked when drying. No shared official group name, pottery mastery, oath or territorial concession. All Talumans continued to respect the inland ochre marker.

No lasting agreement, license, property transfer or fishing right.

diplomacy.first_contact_notes: Tovan explicitly kept the four-person delegation on its side of the stream and avoided implied entry rights, territorial claim or trade treaty. Reciprocal gestures and gifts are a hopeful first contact, not confirmed shared vocabulary. Repeated sounds cannot be reliably interpreted. Day 167 interrupted the V3 advance for the player to decide protocol for three visitors at Taluma boundary. No Taluman group has crossed claimed lands or accepted the closed bundle; no language translation or friendship claim assumed. Day 167 player ordered boundary reception. Esha and Tovan met three visitors in view of villagers, without granting entry. The guests displayed fine dark chipped stone and an ochre-marked woven loop; Taluma provided a small dried-fish portion and fresh water from normal daily supply. Offered small artifacts were accepted as gifts, not a treaty or an established trade route. One visitor made an ambiguous flat-palm response to Tovan’s wooded-swale gesture. Their repeated syllable ("Aru") is not translated. They departed peacefully. No game-day advance for resolution of an encounter already occurring on Day 167. Day 219: Tovan encountered deliberate-looking ochre-cord and stone markers across familiar swale approach, watched by two adults. One made a palm-out gesture, echoing earlier ambiguous interaction. Could mark a boundary, meeting place, warning, or something else. Tovan did not cross; no confirmed ownership, threat, agreement, or shared language. Day 224: Player authorized cautious peaceful approach to interpret the markers without crossing or making claims. Esha, Tovan, Vessa complied. The inland people used stick, cord and palm-out gestures indicating that crossing the marked approach was unwelcome; a separate streamward gesture may offer a meeting alternative, not permission to travel or a treaty. Their acceptance of the displayed old token signals recognition of prior contact, not confirmed alliance. All remain unable to translate speech. Days 225-263: no new formal contact, no trespass beyond the cord, no inferred trade or boundary treaty. Player retains control over sovereign diplomacy. Days 264-291: Acting on player strategic order to seek a mutually beneficial limited sustainable access agreement, Taluma approached only from its permitted side of the ochre boundary in three courteous meetings. Repetition of demonstrations using short dead limbs, living saplings, baskets of fish, four pebbles and a guided path suggested a bounded four-visit escorted deadwood-for-food pilot, not unrestricted woodland access. Key words and precise access terms remain unverified. No party entered past marker, no harvest, treaty, land claim or binding exchange. Stopped for player sovereign decision on whether to authorize a carefully confirmed pilot. Days 292-320: Player authorized a narrow four-visit supervised fallen-wood-for-fish pilot only after renewed clear mutual assent. On Day 295 both parties repeated four-stone counting, fish-basket quantities, dead/live tree contrasts and escorted route gestures; no one entered until both sides assented. Each of four escorted visits was separately accepted and completed; no trees cut, no unescorted access, no territorial claim. The pilot expired after fourth visit and the marked route remains closed absent new mutually confirmed authorization. Days 321-362: Three respectful visits at the ochre boundary increased familiarity and taught a few two-way object gestures, but no verified vocabulary or named nation. The earlier pilot remains expired; no further crossing or trade rights conveyed. Year 2 Days 13-20: voluntary nonbinding craft visit to Taluma by two inland representatives; guests demonstrated clay-tempering/forming and observed Taluman fiber repair. Inland woodland restriction and expired harvesting pilot unchanged. Days 18-25: unrelated (or possibly related; unknown) coastal fishers visibly maintained the Shellbend Cove tidal weir; Taluma did not disturb their work or claim the cove. Year 2 Day 57: Shellbend fishers first met Letha face to face at the outside margin of their working stone weir; reciprocated a coil of cord with a worked shell scraper, while maintaining an unmistakable keep-out signal near fish-trap stones. No territorial claim, shared language, access license or lasting deal. Inland ochre-cord restrictions remain separate and unchanged. Year 2 Days 82-109: Shellbend fishers welcomed limited observation from outside their weir and modeled changing tidal channels with loose pebbles. Letha showed a repair knot and offered a coil of cordage. A fisher may have shared a personal name sounding like "Ami". Trust and understanding improved without new rights or territorial commitments. Inland ochre cord remains separate and closed. Year 2 Days 142-150: both sets of visitors voluntarily attended a short daytime Taluma craft gathering. They appeared to observe each other but mutual political connection, shared language and identity remain unverified. No new binding exchange, boundary crossing, harvest license or treaty. The Taluma lagoon trap remains exclusively within its own grounds. Year 2 Days 305-328: practical counted exchanges using stones occurred only with demonstrated mutual consent, without extending either community’s rights or territory. No new treaty entered. Year 2 Days 353-Year 3 Day 2: two voluntary visits to a small Taluman trading ground; one Shellbend exchange rejected because fish was damp, later sound goods inspected and accepted. Inland visitors offered clay-temper samples at separate mutually accepted barter. No treaties, fees, border crossings or standing access rights. Year 3 Days 12-49: Shellbend and inland visitors participated in nonbinding, inspected quantity demonstrations at Taluma trading ground using a single optional reference basket. No imposed conversion rates, permanent dues or treaty. Day 42, two willing Shellbend adults and their child moved personally to Taluma within spare shelter capacity; this does not grant Shellbend harvesting rights or bind the Shellbend community. Year 3 Day 249: with Sena and willing Shellbend hosts inviting them, Letha and Arel visited only shown Shellbend household area, not the fish weir; reciprocal roof/raised-mat techniques demonstrated. Day 272: with explicit player direction to visit other villages AND new one-off host permission at ochre line, Tama and Kelan made a single escorted round trip to inland household structures, learned replaceable wall panels and ground drainage, then returned. Escort and entry permissions EXPIRED; the old four-visit deadwood pilot remains expired. No rights, claims, treaty or automatic repeated visit. Year4 Days271-298: cautious third-community coastal contact at Reedmouth Inlet beyond Longbank Terrace. Both sides greeted from nonworking open sand, met twice and traded one cordage coil for one bone awl after inspection. Reedmouth label is provisional, group self-name unknown, no land or route permission inferred. Year5 Days171-172: Hall hosted four consenting visiting adults from Reedmouth, Shellbend and the inland stream; all returned home. Guests retained the right not to share work details; no transfer of access rights or binding diplomacy. Year5 Days149-190: Northfold seasonal users permitted four escorted visual watches, no extraction and no right to return after final visit. Year7 Day156: two adults of previously unmet Upper Path traveling community (Taluman provisional label) met at Reedmouth-hosted neutral shore under specific invitation. Voluntary item swap and handoff demonstration suggest greenstone travels through multiple intermediaries, not identified original source. No route, right to entry, extraction, pact or migration. Year7 Day242: Upper Path follow-up mediated by Reedmouth with voluntary stonecraft teaching. Scouts now formally plan legal inland travel from Taluma-side ridge and separate invitation-dependent routes beyond it. No ochre-marked boundary crossed; Northfold closed. Year8 Days18-30: Upper Path travelers secured individual consent for farther inland ridge segment and Splitstone Rest; seasonal rest custodians hosted scout lesson, but swelling runoff required early escorted return. No new named peoplehood or trade route established, green stone source unknown, no extraction/territory rights. Year8 Days35-38: two willing Upper Path adults taught craft at Taluma Hall, returned home. Northfold completely closed and “Northfield” does not refer to an established second site. Year8 Days170-182: tentative nonbinding consultations with Shellbend and Reedmouth on how to request emergency refuge if spring severely fails. Neither group offered a fixed shelter quota; they could choose to respond to fresh requests case by case. Day209: voluntary Upper Path water/runoff lesson, no permanent route or known source, no Northfold visit. Year8 Day314: Upper Path guest recognized polished green exchange stone as material passed through multiple inland intermediaries; showed a cloudy green sample on a carried tool resembling it, but could not identify original outcrop. Stone identity/provenance remains unverified; lesson recorded with host attribution and no permission to quarry. Year10 Day117: Farbank green pebble trade after host-approved neutral meeting, five food-days for three naturally loose stones, with a possible later invitation but no permanent rights. No green-stone mining. Year11 Day17: two north-coast paddlers arrive through invitation at Taluma shore market after Shellbend introduction; name/affiliation tentatively heard as Crescent Shoal (unconfirmed). They show fine shell-and-bone fasteners and ask by gestures if they may return next season. Esha allows short witnessed hospitality but grants NO standing trading rights, land access, fishing rights or treaty. Larger seasonal market decision reserved for guiding intelligence. Year11 Day68 Crescent Shoal delegated two craft workers to consented market; tentative mutual intelligibility improved but self-name remains unverified. Day80-91 hosted visit to their tidal inlet beyond Shellbend by six Talumans using host-guided proven craft, no ownership or route rights. Year11 Days131-180 repeating market rhythm agreed as a schedule of potential invited gatherings: Crescent Shoal, Reedmouth and Shellbend may confirm individually each cycle, with no standing landing access, guaranteed price or territorial rights. Day180 consenting northern buyer traded boat fasteners/brace for a Taluman green pendant. Farbank/Upper Path custodians separately allowed one five-person hosted return trade to Splitstone Rest Days142-161, three loose green pebbles exchanged for five food-days, no green ridge visit or extraction. Year11 Days232 and251-257: expanded Taluma market included four host-invited delegations. Two Talumans Hadan/Letha used their own reinforced boat on a first independently crewed short Shellbend trade route with explicit landing invitation and weather hold. Host coastal rights remain intact. Year11 Days277-365 / Year12 Days1-9: No newly discovered civilization: existing Crescent Shoal, Shellbend, Farbank, Reedmouth and Upper Path partners participated under renewed specific permissions. Taluma gained four consenting skilled adult migrants and one child from known communities. Crescent Shoal dangerous tidal passage navigated with explicit pilot escort. No exclusive trade, automatic unrestricted ports, resource claims or coerced relocation. Year13 Days26-31: Reedwing (Letha,Hadan,Tovan,guide Keshu) observed occupied Ternhook inlet; did NOT assume unoccupied coast, waited for local invitation, exchanged modest gifts, departed. Community’s self-name unknown; no standing rights. Possible broader river plume farther north is inference, not surveyed fact. Year13 Days179-214: Ternhook 3rd direct hosted visit and first reciprocal Taluma shore appearance by two consenting visitors. Trial invitation-exchange practice, one modest fish/net trade, language still limited, no automatic landing, fisheries rights or alliance. Year13 Days252-270: Southern Tidefin exploration after explicit atlas correction; Shellbend hosts supplied voluntary pilot Mata for a single invited staging and reconnaissance; first offshore observations at provisional Windcut Bay beyond SOUTHERN Shellbend. No unknown settlement contacted; fishing stakes/smoke indicate possible local users, no landing, claim, assumed water or fishing rights. Year13 Days316-332: first friendly Windcut Bay contact via voluntary Shellbend pilot Mata and local fisher called Vara; visitors approached only after local invitation, exchanged a small fish/net demonstration, neither party established language fluency or persistent permissions. Year13 Day359 later Windcut visit reconfirmed before offshore exploration toward White-Reed Point; permission not assumed for further coast.

standing_orders: The Council of the Shore may independently allocate routine labor and undertake modest reversible improvements within resources; major sovereign or irreversible actions require player authorization.
Council members will review seats seasonally.
Council will maintain regular observation of the spring and ensure carried drinking water for the occupied high-dune shelter until an adequate source is established.

Until both food and heating fuel reach at least 30 days at the current population rate, the council is to prioritize these reserves alongside daily freshwater safety and essential household care; do not consume protected seeds.
Corun will supervise scheduled collection from the protected upper trickle, avoid drawing drinking water from the lower tidally brackish catchment, and continue checking level and taste at high tide.

Following the first attainment of both reserve goals, council is to manage routine allocations to preserve at least 30 current-population days of food and heating fuel where feasible; report shortfalls, depletion and necessary tradeoffs. It may rotate workers to avoid exhaustion.

PERMANENT USER ORDER (Day 55 issued, implemented Days 56-65): The Council of the Shore must autonomously allocate ongoing essential labor for food production/preservation, clean drinking water, shelter and roof maintenance, and firewood collection/replacement; keep these covered every turn without asking for repeat orders. Rotate and safeguard workers, caregivers, children, elders, ill and injured people.

The Council must monitor and seek to maintain at least 30 settlement-days each of edible food and usable heating fuel, automatically shifting flexible labor to avoid or remedy deficits; sustain shelter capacity for everyone and ensure daily safe-water delivery as far as practical. Report unavoidable shortfalls; no guarantee of success.
Retain protected seed stores; investigate improvements to fuel efficiency, woodland transport and resource conservation without presuming benefit or taking sovereign territorial action.

Day 224 diplomatic safety policy: Taluman crews must not cross the ochre-marked woodland approach or assume timber rights there without further mutual understanding; routine fuel gathering should remain on known unmarked coastal-side routes. This is a voluntary no-entry precaution, not recognition of a mapped border or legal cession.

Day 263 player strategy: seek a mutually beneficial, limited and sustainable woodland arrangement through peaceful engagement; respect the ochre-marked no-crossing request; any binding land-use or trade agreement requires explicit player approval. Do not presume shared language or permission from gifts or gestures.

Day 291 player authorized ONLY a four-visit supervised, fallen-deadwood-for-modest-fish pilot conditional on clear, repeated bilateral confirmation before each marked-boundary crossing, with no live-tree cutting, territorial claims or free access. Pilot fulfilled Days 298, 305, 312, 319; no automatic renewal. Council must respect ochre line again.
