Year4 Day175: covered rainfall collection greatly assists intermittent nonpotable cleaning/hand/tool washing, but an isolated roof line held degraded stagnant water. Do not treat captured rain as guaranteed safe drinking supply, robust dry-season reserve or spring augmentation.

Year4 Day175: about a dozen shared pictograms and tallies can communicate short administrative facts but can be ambiguous (full/empty records mistaken); neither spoken names nor complex narrative are faithfully encoded. Full writing remains a long-term research path.

Year4 Day175: newborn Tavi changes population74 and leaves 7 beds, historical spring minimum82 shares gives an 8-share observed buffer, not guaranteed drought safety. Food/fuel approximations are whole-settlement-day equivalents and infant extra usage is fractional.

Year4 Day240: rainwater boiling trials sometimes broke low-fired clay pots or suffered contaminated handling; vigorous boiling can reduce biological risks but is NOT proof roof-collected water lacks all contaminants, and repeated heating consumes scarce winter fuel.

Year4 Day240: the dry archive contains fragile unfired tablets; an early roof leak already destroyed five trials. Maintain dry covered fired exemplar backups and oral witnesses, no false claim of full writing or universally learned symbols.

Year4 Day303: new Reedmouth coastal group is only provisionally identified; no self-name, known permanent village, shared language or territory rights. Contact did not convey access rights. Do not promise regular trade or settlers.

Year4 Day303: careful boiling reduces some water hazards and trial fuel use, but observational results small, pots crack and dirty handling can recontaminate water. Rainwater is episodic and chemical contaminants are untested. Upper spring observed dry low82 shares vs74 occupants remains only normal drinking source.

Year4 Day303: proto-writing family person signs are conventional tokens; one name-sign collision detected and corrected. Do not treat recorded sign as phonetic spelling or independently proven parentage without oral witness.
Year5 Day10: shore path beyond Reedmouth closes in rising tides; outer shoals and unknown smoke source must not be pursued unsafely or treated as a new people or access right.

Year5 Day10: Reedmouth friendship is young; one invited 3-day craft exchange does not prove willingness to trade repeatedly, to join Taluma, to share fishing locations or to enter political commitments.

Year5 Day68: current protected spring provisional dry-flow low79 resident water shares daily for74 users; five-share margin can disappear in a worse drought. Housing81 is not proof of water capacity; no expansion to100 is justified on these observations.

Year5 Day68: seasonal roof water (110 large jugs, only22 promptly boiled/used) is not drought-proof drinking capacity. First-flush diversion, safe heating and clean covered handling reduce selected hazards but cannot demonstrate universal pathogen/chemical safety or safe multi-day storage.

Year5 Day68: Northfold alternate seep remains nonpotable/unqualified with possible human use, uncertain groundwater independence and expensive transport; no rights or settlement implied. Shore tide warnings are imperfect under storms.

Year5 Day129: new larger covered rainwater store is only a seasonal NONPOTABLE buffer; one reed blockage spoiled a batch. Rain quantities measured as jugloads, not resident-day shares; storing or boiling captured rain does not prove overall water safe, independent or available in drought. Increased water heating costs fuel.

Year5 Day129: two Northfold travelers granted only time-limited escorted observational access; no right to divert, sample, build, settle or traverse unescorted. Guides suggest warm-season low flow but translation uncertain. Winter flow is not proof of dependable drought drinking supply for100, nor of exclusive source ownership.

Year5 Day129: Reedmouth repeating invitation protocol is a voluntary custom, not a binding treaty; each visiting party can decline, no future exchange guaranteed. Existing ochre boundary and Shellbend fisheries retain protections.

Year5 Day194: Northfold winter host-escorted flow declines after dry days and may nearly disappear in summer; do NOT count it in potable capacity, access permission ended Day190. Spring low79 shares vs74 demand, dry severe shortage possible.

Year5 Day194: controlled improved clay boil vessels show ~25% lower fuel per usable small batch in limited trials, but three of ten cracked during firing and additional later defects occurred. No community-wide safe or low-fuel drinking system proven.

Year5 Day320: Northfold almost stopped visibly flowing in warm conditions; seasonal reliability failed observation. Do not spend continued labor or diplomacy on it unless instructed. Existing main Taluma spring most recent measured low79 daily resident-shares against75 now residing, leaving only4-share observed margin; dry-season yield not guaranteed. Household treated rainwater not reliably available through drought or safe to store long.

Year6 Day29: main Taluma spring output in observed dry spell decreased to 76 daily shares for75 residents. Positive observed buffer only1, and drought can worsen; no new immigration approval; preserve essential safe drinking and sanitation even if leisure craft work stops.

Year6 Day29: improved sealant integrity is not proof of safe drinking water. One interior resin-coated sample had suspicious smell and was discarded; forbid testing unverified resin inside drinking vessels. Clean lids, short use, careful boiling where possible, no false safety guarantee.

Year6 Day29: children visiting from other communities are accompanied, supervised and not part of resident counts; no compulsory lessons or assumed access/guardianship. Northfold remains entirely closed.

Year6 Day95: routine drinking spring has lowest observed dry flow76 resident shares against75 residents (margin1); seasonal rainwater not dependable through drought, nonpotable catchment peak84 jugloads does not solve 100-resident safe-water requirement.

Year6 Day95: freestanding reed collection screens are vulnerable to high wind. One of two pilots failed; only one wind-braced design remains. Do not site equipment where falling structure could injure people or contaminate drinking catchment.

Year6 Day95: drought share plans can conceal family/health needs if applied as identical household quotas. Council witnessed needs-sensitive essential allocation, complaint and correction process. All experimental drinking treatments remain supervised and promptly used, never treated as proven safe for long-term storage.
Year6 Day95: remote Northfold is fully CLOSED by player direction, with no new approach or survey.

Year6 Day169: main spring historical low76 daily shares for75 residents. A larger rainwater holding capacity of116 JUGS of nonpotable water is not evidence of 100-person potable capacity or water availability throughout drought. Storm and contamination losses still occur.

Year6 Day169: expanded experimental field has bird pressure, uneven rain and immature new plants; do not book the new field as mature yield or divert protected survival seed. If labor is pulled away from fishing/preservation, food-day reserves can fall.

Year6 Day169: household-wide water duty can create inequity if sick people, caregivers, elders or young children are forced into unsafe or excessive work. Protect alternative contribution, nonpunitive waivers, appeal and access to essential water.

Year6 Day245: birth of Neru brings population76 against spring historically observed minimum76 daily shares, giving ZERO observed margin; continued growth without year-round independently verified potable water creates immediate resilience risk. Infant and illness needs may exceed uniform resident-share proxy; council must keep protective allocations and avoid unwarranted settlement invitations.

Year6 Day245: rainwater cistern added40 jugs covered NONPOTABLE capacity but first windstorm leaked at joint; repair not proof of later full-load/strong-storm durability. Never claim watertightness as drinking-water safety.

Year6 Day245: watered crop strips 31 handfuls vs unwatered23, with limited sample and uncontrolled soil variability, so yield benefits and dry-season sustainable irrigation unproven. Protected survival seed2 and household nonpotable collection priorities remain essential.

Year6 Day317: Spring historically measured low76 daily resident-equivalent shares equals76 population, zero margin. Infant/illness demand and drought risks persist despite rainwater storage, which is not reliably potable.

Year6 Day317: trial hand-dug groundwater pits risk collapse, saltwater intrusion, fecal contamination or interception of the same water feeding the spring. One shoreline test responded to tides and was closed; small inland seep not yet safe, independent or sustainable. Never use as potable or increase population without strong seasonal and sanitation evidence.

Year6 Day317: large40-jug cistern cover came loose in a squall; 12 jug-loads discarded due to contamination. Reinforced cover survived one later severe-weather event at ~35/40 fill, but storm and water quality risks persist. No new storage capacity.

Year6 Day317: Sora selected large seed-head grain appears to germinate more often (17/24 vs11/24), but 48-seed matched experiment is small and early environment and selection may bias results. No new crop-scale harvest in this period.

Year7 Day77: population77 exceeds historic dry observed spring floor76 daily resident-equivalent water shares. Actual demand is not uniform, especially infant and caregiving needs. Must protect sanitation, use existing potable store only when verified, and cannot infer growth capacity from rainy-season flow or nonpotable cisterns.

Year7 Day55: inland shallow monitoring site remains moist but nearly ceases flowing in 24 dry days, potential rain-fed perched water or same supply as existing spring. No confirmed independent perennial groundwater yield, potability or safe excavation design.

Year7 Day49: new cistern pattern two24-jug structures passed ordinary follow-up rains after a lid-lift failure; full-load rare coastal storms remain an unresolved resilience risk. Covered tank does not guarantee potable water.

Year7 Day69: selected seeds outperformed smaller-head comparison in small matched trials (12vs8 mature,21vs14 seed-head bundles), but variation, climate, small samples and year-to-year uncertainty persist; not proven genetics, crop domestication or dependable staple food.

Year7 Day181: local raised stone-ringed well test is physically buildable but seep yield is negligible and unverified safe; cannot be used as water for77 people and may share the spring or be perched rainwater. A deeper unsupported pit risks collapse or spring harm.

Year7 Day181: new upland coastal travel guests were met once through Reedmouth; identity, language, original polished stone source and any onward permission unknown; trading observation is not evidence of an invitation inland.

Year7 Day172: seed-group selected advantage narrowed in full-season repeat (51vs49 mature,78vs71 standardized seedhead units), may reflect weather, fertility and bird damage, not proven genetic domestication.

Year7 Day293: paired shallow seep and main spring changes show rainfall sensitivity without proof of hydraulic connection. Extended dry spell leaves seep near zero; well cannot support growth. Spring historical low76 below77 resident proxy demand.

Year7 Day282: selected wild grain appeared moderately better on seed heads (148vs129 units) but irregular salt-wind storm bent exposed rows and plot conditions remain confounded; large scale staple crop premature.

Year7 Day287: interior route beyond known Taluma-used ridge may intersect ochre community boundaries or unfamiliar users, and stonework contact supplies no general passage/territory consent. Need host invitation and safe water/food return provisions before any long-range excursion.

Year7 Day348: spring measured at historic low75 shares/day, below77-person nominal demand, even though rainy weather later improved flow. The population has no demonstrated robust drinking-water margin; essential-first restrictions may require further action.

Year7 Days308-319: Upper Path guided ridge consent expired after one trip; geologic descriptions do not prove quarry rights, fresh drinking-water source, unrestricted path or authority over adjacent communities.
Year7 Day355: windbreak standing-plant advantage82/128 vs67/128 is preliminary; soil, winds and partial lashing failure confound harvest benefits; no mature result yet.

Year7 Day331: historic records double-counted child with two caregiving hearth ties. Census reconciled77. Later tallies should maintain person-level witness verification and prevent child double counts while preserving caregiving context.

Year8 Day74: short rotation of spring water in low-fired covered ceramics provides no new yield or demonstrated microbe-safe weeks-long reserve; contamination/reused vessels may cause illness. Keep short cycle and severe-rejection oversight; spring historic low75 shares/day against77 residents.

Year8 Day24: heavy rainfall upstream swelled a narrow inland crossing despite locally dry weather. Upper Path escort correctly ended trip early; later unpermitted corridor remains dangerous and unauthorized.
Year8 Day74: acquired stonework demonstration cannot reveal where green stone originates or grant quarry/mineral rights. All inland and coast knowledge exchanges require individual consent.
Year8 Day64: Sora windbreak harvested96 vs73 head units with61 vs49 mature plants, plausible benefit but confounded; no staple crop or claim of domestication.

Year8 Day74: “Northfield” may be a mistaken name for Northfold. Because user expressly demands Northfold CLOSED, neither area was reopened; no separate Northfield location exists in known campaign geography.

Year8 Day153: historical low of spring75/day is below77 residents; short-term covered ceramic jars do not erase this chronic water deficit, and boiling does not remove salt/dissolved pollutants or add production.

Year8 Day109: after a jar remained closed beyond short rotation, cloudy water and suspect lid contact prompted rejection despite no visible leak; contamination remains a risk and observations are not microbiological testing.
Year8 Day153: field comparison is only early germination and seedling retention; windbreak shelter, soil and seed effects cannot yet be disentangled and immature crops are not edible harvest.

Year8 Day217 historic main spring min72 resident-equivalent shares/day vs77 nominal demand, a five-share daily gap absent conservation and short-cycle contingencies. Rain temporarily restored flow Day235, dry-season outlook remains poor.

New pottery workshop 24 formed/15 fired/11 passed short-cycle covered-handling checks. Even clean-seeming two-day jar water can harbor biological contamination; no proven safe long-term drinking reserve, heat costs fuel and boiling does not remove all dissolved hazards.

Neighbor emergency refuge is only exploratory. Shellbend has its own limited resources; Reedmouth possible meeting point not a promise of residence. Crossing others territory or forcing household evacuation prohibited.

Year8 Days242-326: Northfold now reopened by user; wet-season trickle and transient after-rain pool exist but dry-season reliability low, unknown potable quality, travel burden and user rights unresolved; no verified incremental drinking capacity for 77 residents.
Emergency visitor accommodation offered only under conditions and is far too small for village-wide water failure; three-night four-person maximum not a promise if hosts lack water.

Travel-ready covered containers resist spills but unverified biological safety and finite turnover; do not say boiling removes salt or all possible environmental contaminants. Most recent measured Taluma spring low72/day vs77 demand.

Year9 Day37: Northfold test transported just six intact jugs after two three-day excursions consuming36 carrier adult-days; 2 jugs lost or rejected, six intact nonpotable test quantities not a dependable supplement to Taluma spring 72 shares/day low vs77 residents.
Food barter, though modest, costs 8 settlement-days from reserves; avoid promises when fish catches decline, and protect 90-day food floor, four care-food days, and emergency seed.
Consent with known seasonal Northfold users cannot establish ownership or permission from uncontacted other users; seasonality and source quality still materially limit usable water.

Water scarcity unchanged: historical spring low72 daily resident-equivalent shares versus77 residents, so nonpotable substitution reduces avoidable spring use but cannot erase essential drinking gap in serious drought.

Initial lagoon-water net-cleaning caused stiffened cordage and one fouled clean-tool shelf; corrected with labeled separate wash surfaces and air drying. Saltwater cannot replace fresh potable water or be used on cultivated edible crops.
Trading food surplus is conditional on catch, drying quality and partner demand. Shellbend declined the proposed batch this chapter; future partners may reject unfit goods or need different goods.
Northfold wet-season observation is not reliable full-season yield; access to Northfold remains by case-specific, revocable local permission.

Year9 Day207: comparative water audits used approximate old instruments and similar but not identical spring flows; 3 fewer nominal daily shares lost through better carry handling may fail under storm/drought. Historical spring low72 remains less than 77-demand, even with zero transfer loss.

Year9 Day207: Farbank traders travel seasonally and cannot promise future deliveries. Uphill exchange routes consume adult-days and food hospitality; trading all surplus would endanger famine resilience.
Year9 Day207: new craft seals reduce visible spills but no stored raw rainwater or Northfold sample is thereby approved for drinking. Northfold flow remains variable with host consent.

Year9 Day261 recorded historically driest spring source70 vs77 residents, Day263 birth increases residents to78; post-repair handling loss estimated2, leaving about68 delivered under dry conditions. A prolonged drought would overwhelm the tiny short-term vessel reserve even if transfers were perfect.

Year9 Day248 covered experimental gradient trough suffered leak, later dust intrusion at seam/cover and was never approved for drinking; homes on upper dune cannot be served by gravity without higher head or mechanical carrying.
Year9 Day236 Farbank exchange network depends on episodic host introductions; the green stone remains of unknown material/verified origin, and trade cannot conjure guaranteed water.

Year9 Day321: ten-person expedition consumed 180 adult working-days across 18 days, crowding out nonurgent ceramic, drainage and field improvement work; cannot assume such a large team can be sent continuously.

Year9 Day327: green stone was found naturally rounded among Farbank-used Green Gravel Reach stream pebbles, but the actual original deposit and mineral identification are still unverified and upstream access explicitly withheld.
Year9 Day338: experimental enclosed clay conduit improved leakage from3 to1 jug in comparative 12-jug transfer but seams are hard to inspect and clean; not drinkable-water infrastructure.
Year9 Day327: no neighbor can guarantee a long dry-season potable supply for78 residents; Northfold seasonality/rights and spring minimum70 still pose systemic risk.

Year10 Day21: host-guided wet climb near upstream green-bearing exposure presented loose-rock and slip hazards; group withdrew after localized rock movement without injury. Fresh access permit required, no stone extraction authorization.

Year10 Day48: six-section enclosed 12-pace nonpotable gravity conduit delivered23/24 jugs on improved run but water film and a hairline crack discovered in cleanout, requiring removal and repair; potable application unsafe/unvalidated.

Year10 Day64: historic spring minimum70 nominal daily shares for78 residents remains unresolved; higher village homes cannot be served by passive downward-only gravity channel; costly firing and labor limit scale.

Year10 Day117 green stone traders may not have renewable quantity or regular access; fewer stones than Taluma can preserve as food. Their host custodians may withhold future offers; mineral value/identity uncertain.

Year10 Day138 modular clay channels reduce immediate nonpotable transfer loss, but joints accumulate residue in standing conditions, require frequent time-consuming cleaning (~1 adult-day per full dismantle), can crack, and only serve lower sites; no safe potable breakthrough.

Year10 Day148 population79, housing81 (two spare); historic spring lowest70 daily shares, still below essential needs; no guaranteed second safe freshwater source. Population expansion remains water-limited.

Year10 Day226: village79, housing83 but main spring historic drought minimum70 resident-equivalent shares and no demonstrated extra drinking supply; improved sleeping room does not resolve potable bottleneck.

Year10 Day219: even drained, modular nonpotable conduit seal weaknesses and damp residue recur; full cleanout uses ~0.4 adult working-day and may erase water-carrying labor savings. Never infer potable validation.

Year10 Day212: one green-stone ornament took12 craft adult-days and has unknown desirability, wear, and mineral hardness; converting too much food or stone to untested prestige products could be wasteful.

Year10 Day287: another short dry interval showed ~73 spring-output shares/day and~72 delivered after collection improvement versus79 residents; drought contingency may recur, no guaranteed alternate source. Resident growth and future house capacity do not increase freshwater yield.

Year10 Day304: routine water challenge RESOLVED for current size. Residual ordinary risk: unprecedented >21-day no-recharge shortage, unsafe raw catchment batches, serious spring failure, or future growth far beyond reserved supply; handle as discrete events, not recurring default crisis. Northfold remains OPEN.

Year11 Day17: an unfamiliar north-coast party wants recurring market access; inviting them may strengthen exchanges but requires consent from Taluma families, existing coastal hosts and potential landing/fishing boundaries. No host status has been granted.
Year11 Day91: north-coast tidal cut has dangerous ebb and weather exposure; small experimental Taluman boat not suitable for long trips yet. Host permissions required for repeat coastal visits.

Year11 Day178: stronger coastal breeze forced return of supervised three-person Taluman craft. Improved protected-water stability does not establish offshore seaworthiness, storm-proof handling, or independent northern-coast rights.
Green ornaments remain labor-intensive and buyer-specific. Farbank loose-stone access and future stone availability depend on fresh consent, not guaranteed production.

Year12 Day9: Wider four-person cargo craft has only passed protected-water trials, not open coastal tidal crossings or surf in strong winds. Pilot and good weather still necessary for northern voyages.

Year12 Day9: Adult consent and infant-care staffing matter to voluntary growth; increasing families also require future housing and sustainable food/fuel and treated water operations. Water-security milestone remains achieved and scaled rather than reset.
Year12 Day9: Green-stone buyers differ by place; Farbank loose pebble procurement is voluntary and not assured, ornaments require several days of work, source rock extraction remains prohibited.

Year12 Days10-97 (88 days): North tidal crossing is hazardous in ebb or bad weather; supervised pilots improving but Year13 long-range beyond Crescent requires stronger proven vessel, provisions and permission; do not assume land beyond is empty or navigable.

Year12 Days10-97 (88 days): Invitation-based market and skilled migration strengthen economy but consent, host limits, storm-safe new housing, childcare and a real food reserve remain binding. No fresh existential water crisis.

Year12 Day187: Long-range coastline remains uncharted beyond Crescent outer headland, and extended storm/tide exposure is materially greater than short Shellbend shakedown. Year13 mission requires suitable weather, host permissions, provisions, rescue/turnback plan; may be shortened by new encountered users. This is manageable exploration risk, not an excuse to defer forever.
Northern coast beyond Ternhook inlet remains unfamiliar, with fog, tidal bars, changing wind and unknown inhabitants; no broad navigation right or reliable second expedition route established.

Seasonal household growth at population102 leaves six built housing places, so monitor occupancy and build from protected two kits before crowding, while care and apprentice training remain protected.

The coastal contact at Ternhook is friendly but fragile: no reliable common tongue, no recurring invitation yet and storm-damaged tidal fishing structures can constrain hosts; further trips require consent and appropriate weather.
Tidefin second-vessel design still has load-stability issues under hard handling, needs formal crew/weather tests and spare replacement braces before northern route qualification.
Tidefin is qualified only for known coast in fair conditions with experienced crew, staging consent and repair measures; storms and farther unknown headlands still dangerous.
Ternhook contacts now have seasonal invitation signals but little mutually understood spoken language; misread trade signals or showing up uninvited could damage friendship.

Year14 Day260: frontier safety preparations are proportionate; unclear southern fish-stake damage and unknown people beyond High-Shelf Rest could be natural or human. Avoid treating unverified reports as attacks or adversaries.

Year14 Day342: despite improved watch capacity, warnings can be misunderstood across dialects; Shore Words short phrases verified only locally. Inland seasonal route beyond Windgrass Hollow remains unpermitted and unknown. Windcut fishing damage most consistent with storm/debris, not a confirmed enemy.

Year15 Day249: Replacement sets reduce unearmarked cordage stocks and workshop capacity. Trust may improve through transparency but an uncertain product may still fail; Windcut test results must be reported, not pre-guaranteed.
chronicle: Year 1, Early Autumn Day 1: Sixty-seven Taluman shore families established Taluma above the tidal flats. A brackish taste in the spring water was reported after two high tides. No projects ordered and no days elapsed.

Year 1, Early Autumn Days 2-7: The guiding intelligence ordered spring investigation, dune surveying, a seasonal elders council, and wood gathering. The lower catchment was found brackish around high tide; an upslope trickle tasted fresh but its volume is uncertain. Scouts marked a sheltered rooted high-dune bench. The council urged water, stores, and shelter in that order. Six days elapsed; food 19 to 18 days, fuel 13 to 19 days, housing unchanged.

Year 1, Early Autumn Days 8-15: The guiding intelligence ordered enhanced fishing/preservation, construction on the high dune, fuel gathering, a permanent delegated council and a coordinated seasonal plan. Seven-member Council of the Shore formed, membership review seasonal; authority confined to routine work, small projects and safety, with major decisions reserved. Four project adults bolstered food efforts, five built one six-person weatherproof shelter on the high dune, and three gathered fuel. Six previously unsheltered residents moved up the dune with carried water. Food reserves rose 18 to 23 days; heating fuel 19 to 20. Spring still unverified, six people inadequately sheltered.

Year 1, Early Autumn Days 16-25: The guiding intelligence prioritized food and firewood to 30-day targets, shelter for six, and spring investigation/protection. Council deployed 4 shelter builders, 3 fishers, 3 fuel gatherers, and 2 spring workers for five days, then shifted the two spring workers to fuel. A second six-person shelter was completed on the high dune, securing basic housing for all 67. A raised upper-seep draw point and runoff groove reduced tidal exposure, although water reliability remains unproven in winter. Food rose 23 to 28 days, fuel 20 to 25 days. Construction and spring works cost 6 poles, 14 reeds, 2 stone loads, 1 cordage coil. Easiest nearby fallen timber is thinning; protected seed unchanged.

Year 1, Early Autumn Days 26-35: The guiding intelligence directed council-led ten-day allocation, priority fuelwood to 30 days, reed gathering, and storm preparations. First five days 5 fuel/3 reeds/3 reinforcement/1 food project adults; last five days three finishers joined fuel crew for 8 fuel/3 reeds/1 food. Fuel rose 25 to 31 days (25 - 10 + 16), clearing target. Food edged 28 to 29 (28 - 10 + 11) with uncertain seasonal fishing. Reeds rose 9 to 17 (9 + 15 - 7); storms repairs cost 4 poles, 7 reeds, 1 stone load and 1 cordage coil. Two upper-dune and three older roofs reinforced. Day 31 brisk squall caused a minor leak in an old roof; patched quickly, no injury or displacement. No population changes; freshwater carried and spring observations continued. Some reeds curing, and more distant deadwood collection requires effort.

Year 1, Mid Autumn Days 36-45: The guiding intelligence delegated the full next ten-day work period to the Council of the Shore. Council assigned 4 project adults to fishing/preservation, 5 to increasingly distant deadwood, 2 to plant-fiber cordage making, and 1 to spring, roof and drainage monitoring. Preserved food rose 29 to 33 days (29 - 10 + 14); fuel held at 31 days (31 - 10 + 10). Two cured reed/rush bundles were consumed to make two new cordage coils: reeds 17 to 15, cordage 1 to 3. Poles 7 and stone 5 unchanged. Water source remained usable during scattered showers; no severe storm, exploration or demographic changes. Both reserve targets attained concurrently for first time, but the fuel hauling burden grows.

Year 1, Mid Autumn Days 46-55: The guiding intelligence ordered exploration farther inland for sustainable wood supplies. Council assigned Tovan and three others to a seven-day survey northwest through the previously unsurveyed scrub fringe. Scouts marked a narrow foot route over gravelly higher ground to a wooded swale about a day outward in good weather with mixed living trees and scattered deadfall, but no harvesting infrastructure or measured sustainable yield; hauling across dunes remains difficult. Weathered chopping-like marks on a fallen trunk suggest uncertain previous use; no neighboring people found. Scout workers joined fuel crew on their return for the final three days. Project labor: days 46-52, 4 scouting/4 food/3 fuel/1 inspection; days 53-55, 4 food/7 fuel/1 inspection. Food 33 - 10 + 12 = 35 days; fuel 31 - 10 + 8 = 29 days, one day below standing target. No demographic or material changes; upper spring still delivers water, old water risks persist.

Year 1, Late Autumn Days 56-65: The player instituted a permanent Council of the Shore mandate to staff food, potable water, shelter care and fuel replenishment independently, with standing 30-day reserve triggers, workload rotation and project-labor reassignment. Over ten days, workers produced food equivalent to 9 settlement-days while consuming 10; fuel collection provided 10 days from the familiar fringe and one from a small inland relay trial while 10 were burned. Ending food 34 days, fuel 30. Two provisional carrying frames and a partly cleared woodland path were tested; one experimental draft-baffled hearth built without verified savings. Stone flakes and old woodworking scars found at the inland swale; no known neighbors or ownership determined. No births or deaths, all 67 remain sheltered.

Year 1, Late Autumn Days 66-75: Council independently maintained essential services while four scouts under Tovan explored beyond the inland wooded swale to a narrow stream. They reported a worn passage, a cold-ash stone setting and an ambiguous possible footprint but encountered no people and claimed no land. Arel completed six paired cooking trials: a single baffle hearth appeared to use about 10-15% less wood in breezy conditions, with no settlement-wide savings credited. Vessa and Nemi started voluntary apprentice rotations; one cured reed bundle became one cordage coil. Food 34 -> 35, fuel 30 -> 31, reeds 15 -> 14, cordage 2 -> 3. No births, deaths or housing change; protected seeds untouched.

Year 1, Late Autumn Days 76-85: Under council-managed ten-day orders, Tovan led four scouts peacefully to the inland stream. They made three limited flow observations and briefly saw two unidentified adults across the water near recent-looking fiber and vegetation traces, without contact, treaty, claims or identified settlement. Arel built and tested two more wind-baffled hearths using two stone loads (4 -> 2), finding variable benefit and a smoky damp-weather failure; no settlement-wide fuel savings credited. Vessa and Nemi broadened voluntary teaching to roof/water procedures and completed one cordage coil from one cured reed bundle (reeds 14 -> 13; cordage 3 -> 4). Sora and a partner explored wild-grass seeds and prepared two tiny sowing patches with locally gathered seeds, not protected planting stock; no harvest or viable agriculture yet. Council maintained 24 essential-service workers and allocated 12 flexible project workers around exploration, hearths, teaching and agriculture. Food 35 - 10 + 9 = 34; fuel 31 - 10 + 9 = 30; protected seed 2, population 67, housing 67 unchanged. Early winter approaching.

Year 1, Days 86-95 (transition to Early Winter): Council kept 24 daily essential workers assigned and managed 12 flexible workers through cautious diplomacy, wild-seed observation, winter planning and reserve hauling. Tovan led four peaceful representatives to the inland stream and on Day 92 exchanged a few dried fish for a small woven loop with two unidentified people, without crossing the water, identifying their community or making an agreement. Sora noted tentative tiny shoots in the darker sheltered wild-grass plot but no sprouts in the other and no harvest; planting season remains unproven. Esha, Nemi, Seli, Corun and Arel drafted a winter survival plan with aspirations toward 40-day buffers, protected water, storm shelter inspections and voluntary maternal/household support contingent on new housing. Food 34 - 10 + 11 = 35; fuel 30 - 10 + 12 = 32; collected 1 pole and 2 reeds (poles 5 -> 6, reeds 13 -> 15), stones 2, cordage 4, protected seeds 2 unchanged. Population 67, housing capacity 67; no deaths, births, new buildings or treaties.

Year 1, Early Winter Days 96-105: Council autonomously preserved survival duties (24 essential plus 12 flexible) while seasonal seven-seat performance review chose Vessa for one voluntarily vacated household seat and named remaining household delegate Maro; Esha, Nemi, Corun, Arel and Seli retained. No constitutional change. Arel retested three existing wind-baffled hearths and tuned one draft outlet with local silt: roughly 8-12% less cooking wood under favorable comparable conditions, but damping/smoke and village-wide costs unresolved, so no fuel-discount credited. Sora recorded several cold-stressed wild-grass shoots in protected plot, sandy plot still weak; no harvest, established planting calendar or use of protected seed. Seli launched voluntary maternal/infant-care mentorship, but housing at 67/67 and no pregnancies/births. Council pursued 40-day winter buffers: food 35 - 10 + 11 = 36, fuel 32 - 10 + 12 = 34; both above mandatory 30-day minima but below 40 aspirations. Materials unchanged (6 poles, 15 reeds, 2 stones, 4 cordage), seeds 2, population 67, no deaths. Upper spring and high-dune water carrying maintained; no foreign contact this turn.

Year 1, Early Winter Days 106-115: Following the user’s instruction to prioritize both 40-day winter buffers, repeat winter hearth testing, gather future housing materials, and prepare for voluntary household expansion, the council sustained essential service labor. Supplemental crews of 4 on food, 5 on wood fuel, 2 on housing material collection and 1 on hearth trials, in addition to 24 essential adults, brought food from 36 to 40 (10 consumed, 14 preserved) and wood fuel from 34 to 39 (10 burned, 15 collected). Straight poles rose 6 to 9; reed bundles 15 to 19 but some need curing; stone 2, cordage 4, protected seed 2 unchanged. Arel tested three hearths, two roughly 9-11% lower cooking-wood consumption in sheltered cold-weather trials while the third smoked badly in crosswind; no whole-village fuel discount credited. Seli and Arel planned, but did not build, optional 6-place high-dune shelter requiring 6 poles/12 dry reeds/1 stone/1 cordage. Council insists on maintaining emergency repair stock of 4 poles/8 dry reeds/1 stone/1 cordage, so at least one more pole and dry reed bundle and water/wind readiness are needed. Population and housing 67/67, no pregnancies, births, deaths, nor inland contacts this period; water carry routine sustained.

Year 1, Mid Winter Days 116-125: Under standing authority, the Council of the Shore managed ten days without new player-directed projects. A brief squall paused fishing, caused one roof leak (repaired using one cured reed bundle), and spoiled one day-equivalent of stored food. Food went 40 - 10 eaten + 10 prepared - 1 spoilage = 39 settlement-days. Fuel went 39 - 10 burned + 11 gathered = 40; winter wood buffer briefly met. Labor also brought in 2 new straight poles and 2 reed bundles, with some reed stock still curing. No new shelter built, no claimed woodland, contact, childbirth, or fuel-efficiency credit. Population 67, housing 67/67, seed protected.

Year 1, Mid Winter Days 126-135: Following six simultaneous orders, council maintained 24 essential posts and stage-shifted twelve flexible workers between protective raised fish-drying canopy, freshwater flow checks, curing/marking optional family house, repeat hearth comparisons and reinforced inland carrying-frame trial. Food went 39 - 10 consumed + 12 preserved = 41 days, without newly measured spoilage; fuel went 40 - 10 burned + 8 routine haul + 1 trial relay = 39, with no general hearth discount. One additional straight pole and three new wet reed bundles gathered; two poles/three cured reeds/one cordage spent on raised canopy, one pole/one cordage on reinforced frame, leaving 9 poles, 20 reeds (17 cured, 3 damp), 2 stones, 2 cordage, 2 untouched seed equivalents. Corun observed sufficient upper-seep winter draw for the 67 and test allowance for six extra on ten mornings, requiring an extra future carrier, but no long-term drought or water-safety claim. Planned third house site leveled, not built due shortfall of 1 pole and 3 cured reeds against construction + emergency reserve standard. Three hearths remain research prototypes, crosswind smoke in third unresolved. Population/housing 67/67, no births, deaths, diplomatic contact or livestock.

Year 1, Late Winter Days 136-145: Council continued ordinary survival and protected 30-day minimum reserves. Three damp reed bundles began curing toward the future house; workers gathered additional straight poles. No diplomatic contact.

Year 1, Late Winter Days 146-160: Cured reed and pole prerequisites satisfied while guarding 4 poles, 8 dry reeds, one stone load and one cordage coil for emergency work. Arel’s crew completed the previously authorized third six-person high-dune shelter by Day 160; total capacity 73, residents 67. Water deliveries and careful spring monitoring continued. Hearth experiments remained tentative, cultivation yielded no food.

Year 1, Late Winter Days 161-167: Fishing/shellfish and fuel gathering maintained the settlement; cumulative 32-day period from Day 135 ended with 40 food-days and 38 fuel-days. On Day 167, three inland people appeared near Taluma’s outer shelters; one wore an ochre-red wristband and showed braided fiber, apparently requesting contact. The player’s guidance is needed on how to receive them. No access, territorial permission or treaty presumed.

Year 1, Late Winter, Day 167, no additional day advanced: In response to the guiding intelligence, Esha and Tovan met three inland visitors at Taluma’s outer boundary without admitting them to the village. Visitors unwrapped small dark flaked stone items and an ochre-marked cord loop; Taluma offered water and a modest amount of dried fish counted within normal day provisions. Gifts exchanged; no established speech, treaty, trade obligation, woodland access, territorial concession or identification. A flat-palm gesture as Tovan gestured toward the swale remains ambiguous. Visitors walked back inland peacefully before sunset. Resources unchanged (food 40, fuel 38, population 67, housing 73, poles 6, reeds 12, stones 1, cordage 1, seed 2).

Year 1, Late Winter Days 168–187: Council governed food, water, rest, housing and fuel autonomously. Produced 19 food-days, gathered 21 fuel-days, consumed 20 days of each. Voluntary apprenticeships and safe hearth tests continued. No further formal diplomatic mission.

Year 1, Late Winter Days 188–207: Rain damaged a fish storage cover and spoiled 1 food-day; repair cost one pole and one cured reed bundle. Otherwise produced 20 food-days and gathered 19 fuel-days against 20-day consumption. Council managed without sovereign intervention.

Year 1, Early Spring Days 208–219: Sora observed improved leaves on surviving wild-grass trial plants but still no harvest; ordinary fishing resumed modestly. Gathered 13 food-days and 11 fuel-days against 12 consumed. By Day 219, food 39, fuel 37, population 67, shelter 73. Tovan discovered newly placed ochre cord and stones across the inland gathering route, with two observers beyond, including a palm-out gesture. The council suspended crossing the line without asserting its meaning. Player guidance is needed for diplomatic approach and land-use rights; no one crossed or used force.

Year 1, Early Spring Days 220-224: At player direction Esha, Tovan and Vessa made a peaceful, unarmed diplomatic approach to the ochre-cord marker and did not cross it. Two inland watchers used repeated flat-palm and stick-over-cord demonstrations that strongly suggest the marked path is not to be entered. An additional gesture pointed along a route toward the stream, possibly suggesting a safer meeting place. Vessa displayed the old woven token and one visitor responded by touching an ochre wrist band. No common speech, title claim, trade deal, treaty or permission to cut wood was established. Delegation returned safely; Taluma continued avoiding corded inland routes. Council produced 6 food-day equivalents and gathered 4 fuel-day equivalents against 5 days consumed of each, yielding food 40, fuel 36; all other resources and population unchanged.

Year 1, Early to Mid Spring Days 225-244: Council maintained autonomous food, water, shelter and care. Preserved 21 food-days, one spoiled after damp weather; gathered 18 fuel-days while consuming 20. Sora observed wild-grass plot recovery; Arel refined two hearth baffles and left the smoky prototype off limits. Ochre cord respected.

Year 1, Mid Spring Days 245-263: Sora found first tiny seedheads on surviving wild-grass trial plants, observational only and no edible yield. Vessa recognized Iren as independent ordinary cordage maker. Rema and Jorin, previously counted adults, formed a new household in the already built six-person high-dune shelter. Rema privately reported likely early pregnancy; no births or deaths or guaranteed outcome. Two hearths entered supervised daily cooking and saved a measured one settlement fuel-day equivalent in days 255-263; third remains unsafe. Total 39-day accounting: food 40 -39 +43 -1 spoilage =43; fuel 36 -38 actual burned +35 collected =33. Poles 8, reeds 16 (12 cured), stone 1, cordage 3, protected seed 2. No new foreign contact, treaty, or boundary crossing.

Year 1, Late Spring Days 264-277: Player directed peaceful negotiation for limited sustainable inland timber access, preserving ochre no-crossing and user approval for binding terms. Tovan and Vessa opened gentle discussion from the Taluma side; gestures and exchange tokens helped distinguish fallen branches from standing saplings. No shared language and no crossing. Council maintained food and fuel, measured first 14 days food 43 -14 +15=44, fuel 33 -14 +13=32.

Year 1, Late Spring Days 278-291: Follow-up boundary discussions brought Esha to a cautious meeting. Four stones, dead limbs, fish baskets, and a narrow guided approach suggested possible four-visit supervised fallen-wood-for-fish trial. Exact meaning and land rights remain uncertain, no pledge or harvest made. Esha paused for immortal intelligence approval of any binding access arrangement. Second 14 days food 44 -14 +14=44; fuel 32 -13 actual burned +12 legal coastal harvest=31 (1 verified fuel-day cooking saving). Population stays 67, capacity 73; materials unchanged. Day 291 final checkpoint.

Year 1, Late Spring Days 292-296: Player approved a four-visit supervised deadwood-for-preserved-fish pilot, requiring clear mutual assent before any crossing and no live cutting or land claims. On Day 295 Esha, Tovan and Vessa held an extended boundary demonstration with four stones, four fish baskets, fallen and living branches, and one escorted route. The inland representatives repeated the arrangement, affirmed it, and indicated the route. No crossing occurred before mutual consent was confirmed.

Year 1, Early Summer Days 297-320: Four escorted visits on Days 298, 305, 312 and 319 collected 3, 2, 2 and 2 settlement-days of fallen timber, with one modest preserved-fish basket paid per visit (total two settlement-days of food). A guide stopped an attempted reach toward a rooted branch; the worker withdrew and no live cutting occurred. On Day 319 the guides escorted the fourth party out and access expired. The groups remained peaceful; no named nation, shared language, land claim, treaty or automatic renewal. 29-day accounting food 44 -29+30-2=43; fuel 31-28+26+9=38. Taluma population 67, housing 73. Rema possible pregnancy unconfirmed; no births/deaths. Agriculture seed trials and apprenticeships continue, no harvest credited.

Year 1, Early Summer Days 321-339: Player adopted four concurrent priorities: peaceful inland relations, larger wild-grass trials, coastline exploration, and independent sustainable fuel. Council preserved essential labor while Sora cleared three comparative seedbeds. Vessa and Tovan held a first respectful ochre-line meeting; none crossed. Arel began wider safe cooking comparisons. Food and fuel ledger accounted in aggregate over 42 days.

Year 1, Mid-to-Late Summer Days 340-362: Letha and a small shore party skirted the outer headland and identified sheltered Shellbend Cove, possible maintained low-tide stone fish barrier, clay seams, driftwood and risky offshore shoals; no harvest, claim or inhabitants identified. Sora7s mulched bed shows uneven first germination while sandier trials lag; no edible yield or protected seed used. Three nonbinding ochre-line meetings total gave both parties working signs for fish, water and fallen wood, and the neighbors displayed a hard-fired-looking clay vessel; no word meanings or binding pact confirmed. Two safe hearths plus a modest sheltered shared-cooking space produced 2 measured fuel-day equivalents of saving, but local gathering still falls slightly short of consumption. Rema7s possible pregnancy is supported privately without assuming birth. Accounting: food 43-42+48-1 spoilage-1 gifts=47, fuel 38-(42 baseline-2 savings)+39 permitted coast=37. Population 67, housing 73.

End Year 1 Days 363-365 to Year 2 Day 1 (3999 BCE): Taluma completed its first full year and transitioned to Year 2 with no forced leadership review, demographic jump or major rule change. Esha and residents recalled the first landing in an informal oral gathering. Council kept food, water, fuel, shelter and care staffed.

Year 2 Days 7-17: Tovan and Vessa invited neighboring inland craftspeople with repeated gentle signs at the ochre marker. Two guests voluntarily reached Taluma for a daytime nonbinding exchange: Vessa and Iren demonstrated fiber repair while an inland guest demonstrated clay tempering and hand shaping. Food hospitality totaled one settlement-day equivalent across the period. Guests left peacefully with their own vessel. Taluman trial cup cracked before firing. No treaty, crossing rights, official group name or ceramic breakthrough.

Year 2 Days 18-25: Letha visited Shellbend Cove on two falling tides and confirmed stone fish-weir use by at least two adults and a younger individual. One open-handed greeting was returned from a distance. Scouts neither approached within the fishing works nor took materials, installed shelters, or assumed rights. Coastal users remain unnamed and not confirmed connected to the inland stream group.

Year 2 Days 1-32: Sora obtained only a tiny bowl-sized sample of mature seed from the previous tiny patch for planting research, while three comparative larger beds matured unevenly; no food-day yield or protected-seed consumption. Rema remains under voluntary pregnancy-related care with no birth; population 67, housing 73. Accounting for 35 days: food 47-35+38-1 hospitality=49; fuel 37-(35 baseline-2 measured savings)+34 lawful gathering=38. Poles 9, reeds 16, stone 1, cordage 5, protected seed 2.

Year 2 Days 39-71: Maro and Vessa established a Circle of Witnesses gathering near each observed moon cycle. Witnesses distinguish direct experience from passed-down stories; cord and tidal tally markers aid memory but do not amount to writing. Esha approved regular recitation. Early arguments about storm timing were preserved as competing accounts.

Year 2 Days 43-57: Letha and companions approached Shellbend fishers without entering their fish-weir work area; after cautious repeated greetings, one adult fisher accepted a single coil of cord and gave a shaped shell scraper. No access, trade contract, territorial claim or verified group name.

Year 2 Days 48-67: Vessa, Iren and Arel shaped seven small local-clay vessels with crushed temper, slow drying and careful outdoor pit firing. Two survived cooling; one held water briefly but gradually seeped. Limited proof of firing clay, not dependable pottery stores. One extra settlement-fuel-day spent.

Year 2 Days 33-74: Sora retained small experimental planting seed samples, strongest from mulched dark soil; no food yield credited. Rema received private voluntary care, no births or deaths. Council maintained regular food, water, fuel and shelter work. Food 49-42+44-1 gift-1 spoil=49; fuel 38-(42 baseline-3 hearth savings+1 pottery firing)+38 permitted local gathering=36. Housing 73, population 67, protected seed 2.

Year 2 Days 120-160: Nemi and Letha trialed a small, removable local lagoon tidal fish guide with a woven trap. Initial high tide disrupted stones; after revision, the pilot added approximately 2 food-day equivalents of preserved catch. No Shellbend structures were touched or copied into restricted grounds.

Year 2 Days 127-153: Taluma-side headland survey found small workable clay exposure and loose stone. Two stone loads hauled in, one used in reversible lagoon fish guide. Eleven additional low-fired pots tried; six survived, three held water overnight. Firing used 2 fuel-days in addition to ordinary baseline; no high-temperature kiln.

Year 2 Days 142-150: a coastal fisher and an inland clay worker each voluntarily visited Taluma for a limited nonbinding gathering of craftspeople, showing tidal-flow model and tempering techniques. Talumans exchanged cordage and drying knowledge. Their relationship to one another remains unknown. Both departed peacefully. No treaty, restricted passage or land claim.

Year 2 Day 160: Population 68 (including infant Nala) and 73 places. Food 48 -41 +44 -1 hospitality = 50. Fuel 35 -(41 baseline -3 hearth savings +2 pottery firing) +39 permitted gathering =34. Poles 8, reeds 16, stone loads 2, cordage 4; protected seed 2. Winter operations continue normally.

Year 2 Days 161-205: Two additional removable tidal guides/creels tested within Taluma lagoon, one displaced in a winter surge and reset. Experimental fishing added about 3 food-day-equivalents inside normal production. Leni, a younger observer, raised the issue of small fish; Nemi began a hand-release test with no claimed proven ecological effect.

Year 2 Days 168-198: Arel directed a marked carrying route between Taluma and already surveyed Taluman-side headland clay/stone, bringing 3 local stone loads and preparing 3 clay basketloads without crossing Shellbend or ochre-cord restrictions. New route remains hazardous in high tides.

Year 2 Days 174 and 199: Vessa hosted two voluntary nonbinding small craft sessions; willing inland and Shellbend visitors shared practical skills at different gatherings, without implied alliance, access, or shared group identity. Potter trials: 10 attempts, 6 intact, 4 held water overnight.

Year 2 Day 182: Taluma adopted voluntary Open Learning Days, with older children and young apprentices learning basic knotwork, safe clay forming, planting observations, tide marks from shore and Circle of Witnesses history. No formal writing or compulsory child labor.

Year 2 Day 205: 68 inhabitants, 73 housing places, 51 food-day reserve and 34 fuel-day reserve. Materials 9 poles, 16 reeds, 4 stone loads, 3 coils of cordage, 3 prepared clay basketloads; protected seed 2 unchanged. All settlement consumption reconciled for 45 days.

Year 2 Days 206-246: Following the player’s additional strategic instruction, Corun and rotating scouts searched Taluma-side gullies and western dunes for a fallback water supply. Two wet depressions yielded stagnant brackish runoff or quickly dried, while a third shallow western trickle flowed briefly after rainfall. Water tasted fresh but no reliable potability or year-round independence was proven; a small clay-lined basin cracked. The protected upper seep remains Taluma’s only confirmed daily source.

Year 2 Days 213-239: Arel, Vessa, and limited rotating crews erected an open-sided reed-roof Hall of Many Hands using six poles, nine cured reeds, one stone load and two cordage coils. Adult essential services continued, some hauling and pottery work were temporarily slowed. Construction completed Day 239 with no housing capacity change; modest maintenance added to standing council duties.

Year 2 Days 242-244: The Hall of Many Hands hosted voluntary Open Learning Days with older children, adult apprentices, Maro’s oral chronicle, and demonstrations of fish-trap knots, clay shaping, water observations, and plant seedlings. A willing Shellbend fisher and an inland clay worker each visited on separate daylight sessions. No trade concession, land access, treaty, uniform language or new permanent residence was inferred; visitors were free to leave.

Year 2 Day 246: 68 residents, including infant Nala, 73 housing places; food 51 settlement-days, fuel 32 days. 41-day food: 51−41+43 preserved−1 hospitality−1 spoilage=51. Fuel: 34−39 actually burned+37 lawfully gathered=32; 4 cooking-fuel-day savings and 2 extra pottery-firing fuel-days included in actual burn. Material stocks 8 poles, 16 reeds, 4 stone loads, 2 cordage coils, 3 prepared clay baskets, 2 protected seed equivalents. No deaths, births, or unauthorized boundary crossings.

Year 2 Days 247–274: Under explicit player priorities, Corun organized two small experimental rainwater collectors using stones, clay, reeds and repair labor. The shallow dune clay-lined pit cracked again and lost most of its water. A sheltered roof-runoff catchment held rain after spring showers but acquired windblown leaves and sediment; designated nonpotable workshop/cleaning supply only. Corun and Leni kept simple tide/rain observations and made no claim of an independent safe drinking source.

Year 2 Days 253–281: Esha, Vessa and Maro extended invitations through ordinary peaceful contacts. On Day 281, Taluma hosted the first annual Meeting of Many Hands at the hall, with willing visitors from the streamside inland people and Shellbend coastal fishers. Iren demonstrated strong cordage splices, a coastal guest showed small fish-trap weighting arrangements with model stones, and an inland guest compared clay temper. Young Talumans watched age-appropriate sessions, including Leni; no binding treaty, marked woodland access, fishing rights or new territorial claims. Guests left freely; next yearly gathering is only a plan, not a guarantee.

Year 2 Days 247–290: Routine council maintained 24-person survival staffing, diverted flexible adult crews to emergency fuel recovery and two rainwater trials while continuing limited agricultural and ceramic testing. Food 51−44 eaten+49 preserved−2 hospitality−1 spoilage=53 days; fuel 32−42 actual burned+44 lawful collected=34 days (44 baseline burn−4 verified safer hearth savings+2 pottery fuel). Population 68 including infant Nala, housing 73, no births/deaths or migration, 2 protected seed equivalents unchanged. Final materials 8 poles, 16 reeds, 3 stone loads, 2 cordage coils, 2 prepared clay basketloads.

Year 2 Days 291-318: Esha asked Letha, Vessa and Maro to develop clear, nonbinding barter practice with willing neighbors. At Shellbend, paired stones were used to show quantity and exchange expectations; a coastal fisher could examine goods and refuse without penalty. A small trial exchange of preserved fish for two shell scrapers was mutually confirmed without touching or entering the active fish-weir.

Year 2 Days 312-328: At an unrelated voluntary meeting on the Taluma side of the existing ochre woodland marker, Iren offered a sound cordage coil, and an inland visitor offered two ochre stones. Both repeated a counted exchange and accepted it; no one crossed the boundary. Maro and older learners started teaching witnessed quantities, inspection and mutual refusal as a Taluman custom, not imposing it on either neighboring people. One-day food equivalent traded at Shellbend, one-day food equivalent hospitality across meetings, one-day spoiled during damp preservation, all in resource accounting.

Year 2 Days 301-333: Corun and two rotating scouts pushed west beyond the old rain-fed trickle, found the Western Gravel Run beneath a stony shelf about half a day from Taluma and observed moving water on three checks, including a return after ten days without substantial rain. Their observations suggest better persistence than the shallow dune seep, but water safety, late-dry-season flow, catchment independence, route security and carrying cost are unresolved. No drinking-water access or claimed territory. Leni helped compare tide, rainfall and water marks during supervised learning back in Taluma.

Year 2 Day 333: Council survival crews stayed staffed while small teams surveyed west and conducted nonbinding trade demonstrations. Population 68 (including Nala), housing capacity 73, food 55 (53−43+48−1 trade−1 hospitality−1 spoilage), fuel 37 (34−41 actual burned+44 legal gathered). Actual fuel burn is 43 baseline−4 efficient cooking savings+2 controlled pottery firing. Raw materials 8 poles,16 reeds,3 stone loads,2 cordage coils,1 prepared clay basketload; protected seed 2. One new coil made and one bartered; reeds gathered balanced fiberwork and roof repair. No deaths, births, war, treaties, prohibited boundary crossings or drinking use of unverified water.

Year 2 Day 338: Esha charged Corun to examine Western Gravel Run for an outpost only on paper; no settlers, posts, water diversion, claim or boundary crossing authorized. Council scheduled a small survey around ordinary survival shifts.

Year 2 Days 346-359: Corun and Tovan visited a gravel bench west of Taluma. Lodged dead branches high along stream edges suggest occasional floods; the run weakened after dry weather though still moved. A half-day walk and uncertain water security make immediate settlement imprudent. Scouts marked observations, not a claim.

Year 2 Day 353: Maro and Vessa opened a modest removable awning with exchange mats beside the Hall of Many Hands. Visitors from Shellbend and inland groups could inspect counted fish, cordage, small craft materials and refuse freely; council supplied no universal weights or official prices.

Year 2 Day 362: a Shellbend fisher refused a damp fish basket. Nemi honored the refusal and had the suspect goods removed from trade; a later nonbinding exchange succeeded when properly preserved fish were inspected. The mishap strengthened the witnessed inspection practice rather than creating a quarrel.

Year 3 Day 2: Village completed its second year and began a third. The next voluntary trading gathering drew a few willing visitors who inspected goods and accepted one-time exchanges; no treaties, market monopoly or territorial agreement. Nala now crawls under close family supervision; population remains 68.

Year 3 Day 4: Council report: 68 residents in 73 housing places, food 56 days (55−36+40−2 traded−1 hospitality), fuel 38 days (37−34 actual burn+35 lawful gathered). Actual fuel consumption 36 baseline−3 measured cooking savings+1 pottery firing=34. 8 poles, 16 reeds, 3 stones, 2 cordage coils, 2 prepared clay baskets, and 2 protected seed equivalents. The west outpost is only a studied possibility; main spring remains only working daily safe-water point.

Year 3 Day 12: Maro and Leni noticed that two visually similar baskets could contain different amounts. Volunteers agreed to compare filled volumes with one Taluman reference reed basket and counted stones, inspect goods and permit refusals; the practice was not imposed on visitors.

Year 3 Days 15-35: scouts compared Western Gravel Bench and other possible outpost ground. A north-coast raised bench called Longbank Terrace had firmer roots and no obvious recent flood debris, but a small seep was unverified for drinking or dry weather and the site may be used by others; no occupation or claim.

Year 3 Days 20-44: Vessa and Iren conducted fourteen small vessel/storage-lid trials. Eight survived firing; three fitted lids were useful for sheltered, short-duration DRY seed storage, but a damp-weather crack and porous walls prevented claiming year-long safe food storage. Three additional fuel-days expended on pottery firing.

Year 3 Day 36: Esha and Seli invited willing visitors to consider joining Taluma as residents, explaining that the village could support only a small household with existing housing and the working main spring; no demands on neighbor communities or exclusive labor terms.

Year 3 Day 42: Sena and Daro, two adult craftspeople from Shellbend, and their six-year-old child Tiri freely moved into spare shelter in Taluma. Population 68→71 (42 adults, 22 children, 7 elders), housing remains 73. Shellbend fishery rights remain with Shellbend residents as a group; no covenant or territory transferred.

Year 3 Day 49: council accounts for 45 days and small late-arriving population increase. Food 56 old-population settlement-days to approximately 54 new-population days after 45 baseline days eaten, 49 preserved, 3 days paid in exchange/hospitality/spoilage and newcomer consumption. Fuel 38 old-population days to 37 new-population days after 44 baseline adjusted burns (45 baseline−4 hearth savings+3 pottery), 45 lawful collections and newcomers. No seed reserve consumption, births or deaths. Materials 9 poles, 16 reeds, 4 stone loads, 2 coils and 2 prepared clay basketloads.

Year 3 Days 55-82: after the arrival of Sena, Daro and Tiri left only two spare beds, Esha and Arel directed ordinary crews to build two four-place family shelters on Taluman high dune. No outpost founded; all weatherproof work paid in poles, reeds, lashings and labor.

Year 3 Day 70: Corun demonstrated the difference between having enough drinking water today and having a dependable second spring. The Hall of Many Hands learners measured spring drawing and learned that western trickles and roof runoff were not authorized drinking sources.

Year 3 Day 91: Tama and Kelan, independent adult craft visitors from inland stream people, freely chose to become Taluma residents after the council established sheltered places and measured normal-season spring draw. Taluma’s population became 73; neither community acquired rights over the other.

Year 3 Day 103: the council tallied 54 days including 12 full days of two new adults, with preserved food and lawful firewood increasing enough to leave ~55 current-population food-days and ~39 fuel-days. No recorded births or deaths. Annual craft meetings, schools, cultivation, tide traps, trade and protected seed continued under ordinary governance.

Year 3 Days 104–164 (restored from the fully narrated previous turn): winter cold and storms; four separate witnessed fuel-for-fish exchanges delivered six settlement fuel-days at the cost of two food-days and one cordage coil. No crossing of the inland woodland boundary, treaty or recurring obligation. Three reversible local tidal traps and raised drying racks improved food output but one trap suffered a winter surge.

Year 3 Day 151: Anet, 23, a fish-preservation worker, and Boran, 25, a shelter-frame worker, freely married with mutual public assent at the Hall of Many Hands. Seli facilitated opt-in adult introductions and household support. No birth or confirmed pregnancy during the 61 days.

Year 3 Day 164: population 73 (44 adults, 22 children, 7 elders), housing 81, preserved food 58 current-person days, fuel 38 current-person days. Documented food ledger 55−61+68−2 traded−1 hospitality−1 spoiled=58; fuel ledger 39−61 baseline+5 hearth savings−4 severe-cold extra−1 pottery+54 lawful gathering+6 exchanged=38. Protected seed remains 2 and untouched.

Year 3 Days 165–189: a cold wind revealed leaks in two high-dune family roofs. Boran argued that future children deserve warmer, drier homes; Tama demonstrated an overlapping reed weave, and Arel tested two sheltered, well-ventilated roof/entry arrangements. One dangerously over-sealed trial caused smoke to gather and was abandoned immediately; no injuries reported.

Year 3 Day 193: first voluntary Roof-Raising Day. Neighbors repaired roofs together, marked completed work with a small braided reed cord and taught children safe lashings and how to recognize damp thatch. The custom explicitly welcomes unmarried adults, elders and visitors; nobody is assigned a spouse or required to have children. Maro records the craft changes and the social meaning.

Year 3 Day 211: Esha convened Corun, Nemi, Tovan, Seli and Arel for a capacity-for-100 study. Taluma currently 73/81: at least 19 more housing places needed, sketch calls for five 4-place shelters (101 capacity), but obtaining proven safe potable water for a 37% population increase is still unresolved. Food/fuel and skilled care must expand too. Council did not authorize construction or major migration.

Year 3 Day 217: at Night of Shared Fires, households told stories of the first winters, births, marriages and fostered care beside a smoke-safe communal hearth; young apprentices publicly showed better storm-roof knots and a dry-fish sorting screen. These rituals create motivation to improve craft without imposing ritual attendance or fertility expectations.

Year 3 Day 229: 65 days elapsed from Day 164; population remains 73 (44 adults,22 children,7 elders), housing 81, eight free. Two warmer roof pilots, no births or marriages this period, no new immigrants. Food days 58−65 consumed+68 preserved−1 hospitality−1 spoilage=59. Fuel 38−65 baseline−5 winter extra+6 proven heating savings−1 pottery+67 lawful gathered=40. Material poles10+2−1=11; reeds15+5−4=16; cordage1+2−1=2; stone4, clay3 and protected seed2 unchanged.

Year 3 Day 249: Letha, Arel and Sena made a specifically invited Shellbend home-building exchange, stayed outside the fish trap and only toured homes shown by hosts. Shared Taluman roof overlap and smoke-vent methods; learned raised woven beds and roof runoff channels. Permission limited to this single visit.

Year 3 Day 259: Corun introduced repeated spring-water-share comparisons using a dependable clay measure. Across a 12-day relatively dry interval, measured output about 86-94 resident-average shares per day, observed low 86. 73 residents are currently supplied, but 100 needs roughly 100 shares per day and no drought-year or water-safety proof exists for larger capacity. Improved spring draw and covering, not physical output.

Year 3 Day 272: willing inland hosts invited Tama and Kelan for exactly one escorted approach from ochre boundary to home-building demonstrations and back. Taluma shared safe roof/ventilation techniques; guests learned removable woven walls, foundation stones and drainage. No wood taken, no new claims, access expired after same-day return.

Year 3 Day 282: Anet quietly told Seli of possible early pregnancy signs. No confirmation or public announcement; Seli offered voluntary care. Population stays 73 and young Nala continues growing normally.

Year 3 Day 290: over 61 days village selected future family-home stockpile rather than building now. Materials P11+7−2=16, reeds16+13−4=25, stone4+2−1=5, cordage2+3−1=4; half of poles and 14 reeds plus 2 stone and 2 cordage earmarked for TWO future homes with curing incomplete, leaving substantial repairs stock. An existing home received one Shellbend/inland-inspired drainage/wall pilot, and spring draw staging was improved. Food59−61+64−1 guests−1 spoil=60; fuel40−61+6 roof/hearth savings−1 pottery+58 lawful wood=42. No birth, death, migrants, new housing, second outpost, treaty, unrestricted entry or loss of protected seeds.

Year 3 Day 309-312: Sena and Boran made one specific invited four-day learning visit to Shellbend households, teaching safe reed-roof vents while studying raised sleeping mats and adjustable rain drainage. Permission expired upon departure. No entry into the active weir, fishing/harvest rights or property transfer.

Year 3 Day 315-319: one Shellbend adult craft teacher voluntarily visited Taluma Hall of Many Hands for a supervised adult builder exchange, demonstrating drainage while Taluma explained safe roof-entrance ventilation. No binding agreement.

Year 3 Day 332-336: Tama and Kelan obtained a new, specific inland invitation and escort for a five-day adult apprenticeship past the ochre marker. Demonstrated layered ventilated roofs and learned replaceable wall lacing and dry footings. Their one-off permission expired with return; customary boundary remains fully active.

Year 3 Day 340-344: one inland craft teacher voluntarily traveled to Taluma Hall for a short reed-panel joint workshop. Locals and older children learned safe assembly techniques; no permanent travel agreement or tuition/compulsory work.

Year 3 Day 354: Corun and Vessa concluded small covered-water storage experiments. Eight fired-vessel attempts yielded five intact, three initial no-leak candidates, then one vessel water became cloudy/odorous during extended storage, leading to disposal. Two covered vessels may be used only in observed daily-refill experiments; this is not reliable multi-day clean-water storage or extra source capacity. In a dry spell main spring measured low 82 resident-equivalent shares daily, enough for today’s 73 but not the 100-person expansion target. Anet privately told Boran pregnancy is possible and Seli continues support. Food60-64+68-1 hospitality-1 spoilage=62, fuel42-64+7 verified savings-2 pottery+62 lawful gathering=45; P16+3-1=18, reeds25+7-3=29, stone5+1-1=5, cords4+2-1=5, prepared clay3+2-3=2. Two-home earmark untouched, protected seed untouched, no population change.

Year 3 Day 365: Taluma ends its third year with 73 residents and 81 housing places, food and fuel well above minimums, but main known drinking spring observed as low as 82 resident-equivalent shares daily. Council reiterates no growth to 100 on assumptions or purely decorative stored-water containers.

Year 4 Days 2-22: Arel, Tama and Boran began a four-home gradual retrofit with removable reed panels, raised dry sleeping areas and stone-edged rain runoff. An early drainage gutter routed rain back toward bedding; corrected after inspection. Future-home building materials remained separately earmarked; no new dwellings.

Year 4 Days 9-37: Corun and Letha systematically compared permitted accessible western and northern water sites. One lower hollow failed through tidal/brackish conditions, another dried out. Northfold Seep beyond Longbank continued to trickle after eleven days without meaningful rain, in a visibly different surface channel. It was neither used nor declared safe, independent, accessible water for village consumption; unknown local use rights respected.

Year 4 Day 24: the Hall of Many Hands began regular named adult apprenticeship paths, with oral witnessed tests of house repairs, food preservation, practical container making, water/tide observations. Learners of any age may observe age-appropriate safe instruction; adults alone perform hazardous tasks and host-approved travel.
Year 4 Day 33: Anet informed chosen relatives that she is expecting a child. Boran continues practical preparations; Seli helps voluntarily. No newborn this turn.

Year 4 Day 47: Council recorded food 62-58+62-1 visiting hospitality-1 spoilage=64 and fuel 45-58+9 safe efficiency savings-1 pottery firing+57 locally lawful collection=52. P18+6-3=21, reeds29+8-5=32, stone5+2-2=5, cord5+3-2=6, prepared clay2+2-1=3. Two-home reserved P8/R14/S2/C2 unchanged. Population73/housing81. No territory claimed, no new water supply credited.

Year 4 Days 50-90: older children including Leni challenged the builders: if roof drains can send water away from bedrooms, can they also send useful rain into a vessel? Corun and Arel approved tiny reversible trials on existing Taluma roofs, keeping spring collection free of runoff contamination.

Year 4 Days 63-104: two small roof-fed rain collectors tried. Dirty first flush and a leaky open basin spoiled early catch. The better covered liner held 20 large jug-loads over three rainfalls, used only for clay mixing and tool cleaning; no drinkability/long-term drought dependability claimed. The upper spring remains only counted village drinking source, historically measured low82 daily shares for73.

Year 4 Day89: Arel, Tama and Boran established five observed building checks: dry slope away from bedding and spring, raised mat, breathable hearth and smoke outlet, replaceable wall, and inspection after actual rain. Three further occupied homes improved, one incorrectly graded outlet corrected. No new capacity; future family home materials preserved.

Year 4 Days 76-107: Maro and Vessa helped Leni convert counting stones and rain-vessel diagrams into a small agreed suite of carved/incised water-roof-container-season marks on clay and wood. Several apprentices recognized the same simple water-tally records without an accompanying teller. This is nascent pictographic proto-writing, not yet a script capable of recording full speech or all Taluman history.

Year 4 Day98: Seli and Nemi established an inspected provisioning reserve for growing families, illness and caregiving. Four stored settlement-days of food earmarked WITHIN 65 total, plus 3 reed bundles and 1 cordage coil from unreserved materials; future new-house earmark P8/R14/S2/C2 untouched. Anet continues pregnancy with care, no birth, death or new settler during period.

Year 4 Day111: ledger for 64 days: food64 -64 consumed +68 produced -1 hospitality -2 damp spoilage=65; fuel52 -64 baseline +10 safe energy savings -2 limited clay firing +60 legal gathering=56. Year4 Day117: player directed further covered rainwater collection and progression from tally symbols toward writing, with continuation. Council maintained all inherited duties and territorial restrictions.

Year4 Days123-155: Arel and Corun constructed more roof-rain feeds and one covered clay/stone central basin, capacity roughly 18 big jugs. Three tested lines, two remain operational; one contaminated/leaking stagnant batch discarded and third line isolated. Across repeated rains 72 large jug loads collected, 54 used for nonpotable washing and clay, 14 lost/discarded and four covered at Day175. No potable water certification or independent drought source.

Year4 Day141: an apprentice misread an ambiguous stored-water tablet as empty vessels rather than filled ones. Leni, Maro and Vessa revised the agreed pictographic signs to distinguish full/empty and water moving in/out, with repeated independent reader checks. Narrow resource records now transmit without live explanation but no phonetic or full language writing.

Year4 Day167: Anet delivered healthy daughter Tavi with Seli and family assistance; Boran supported household and infant care. Population increased from73 to74, housing capacity81, seven vacancies. Maro orally witnessed birth and put a child tally beside the parental household emblem, preserving birth as an event without claiming to inscribe name in phonetic script.

Year4 Day175: 64-day approximate accounting, food65−64 ordinary consumption+69 production−1 hospitality−2 spoilage−8/73 infant incremental =66.89 old 73-person-days (~66 current 74-person-days); fuel56−64 ordinary−3 extra cold+12 measured safety savings−2 pottery+60 legal fuel−small infant extra =58.89 old days (~58 current days).
