Esha rotated Council Listening Bench participation to include Iset, heard Dava defend real resource costs, and maintained seven-member governing authority. Census108, housing113, food294, fuel212.

Year15 Days250-276: Esha expanded the Council Listening Bench to practical supervised work-budget hearings; Dava and Iset had to reconcile fiber manufacturing and testing with net maintenance, boat repairs and family-care hours. Seli ensured caregivers were represented. All seven council seats remained unchanged and no apprentice gained voting power.

Year15 Days277-294: Vessa, Tira and Maren tested multiple cord bindings with marked local samples and repeated wetting/grit contact. Two early closely braided samples loosened; revised knots improved later short tests without establishing storm-season or Windcut-field reliability. Apprentices kept a comparison ledger and produced usable standard cordage while consuming five coils in destructive experiments.

Year15 Days295-307: Dava defended a bounded trial allocation instead of an immediate scale-up; Nemi agreed no speculative Windcut/Reedmouth bulk sale would be booked. Council preserved one future house kit and family care stocks, repaired fleet, and maintained the existing three hide charts. 58 days elapsed, census108/housing113, food300, fuel219, cordage23.

named_people.name: Esha
named_people.role: elder and speaker for the families
named_people.traits: patient, strongly favors keeping the households together
named_people.developments: Convened an autumn council, advocated securing water first, then food and shelter; no permanent new powers were granted. Presided over the founding of the seven-seat Council of the Shore; accepted seasonal review of council membership and limits on major decisions. On Days 16-25 directed the first coordinated prioritization under delegated council authority, accepting that supplies would fall short of 30-day targets while all families obtained shelter. Day 26-35 council managed two-stage labor shift, ultimately reaching the fuel reserve target while food remained one day short; deferred festivities and emphasized maintenance. Days 36-45 chaired a practical maintenance allocation that kept both 30-day reserves at or above target without seeking new powers; pressed the council to account for fatigue on long wood-carrying routes. Days 46-55 organized ordinary reserve work during Tovan’s authorized four-person survey. Council reported fuel shortfall (29 days) instead of pretending the discovered timber was already stored; urged restoring minimum before spending heavily on inland works. Days 56-65 accepted the guiding intelligence’s permanent mandate for a survival labor roster; set out explicit reserve triggers and work rotation rather than requesting repeated authorization. Days 66-75 kept standing food/water/fuel/shelter roster active while allowing scouts and voluntary teaching; insisted the council hear the scouts before any inward land-use expansion. Days 76-85 kept the essential-services mandate intact through six competing orders; cautioned against any inland claim after two unidentified people were sighted. Days 86-95 coordinated ten-day winter and household-support plan while keeping reserve duties staffed; resisted mistaking tentative outsider gestures for a treaty. Day 105: hosted first seasonal seven-seat performance review; maintained delegated powers and permanent survival rosters while accepting an ordinary member rotation. Day 115: balanced food/fuel buffer ambitions with emergency repair stock; celebrated reaching 40 days food but refused to declare winter safe while fuel at 39. Days 116-125 accepted a council labor rotation that prioritized essential stores and winter safety over immediate expansion; reported the food buffer slipping below 40 after a storm. Days 126-135 mediated a dispute between immediate preservation work and long-term housing materials, prioritizing protected drying racks and retaining emergency roof stock despite future shelter delays. Day 167: halted discretionary contact at village edge after three apparent inland visitors approached; sought guiding intelligence direction on diplomatic protocol while survival services remain in council hands. Day 167 personally welcomed three inland visitors at the settlement boundary, without granting entry or accepting a treaty; guests left peacefully. Day 219: on learning of newly placed cord-and-stone markers in the wooded swale, accepted Tovan’s temporary no-entry precaution and referred consequential relations with inland people to the guiding intelligence. Days 225-263: council kept daily survival and project work running without new approvals; Esha declined to cross the marked woodland route and requested longer-run fuel substitution studies. No binding diplomatic steps taken. Days 264-291: personally attended final no-crossing woodland conversation after Tovan and Vessa led first two. Refused to commit or claim access on gestures alone; referred potential escorted deadwood-for-fish pilot for player approval. Day 295 confirmed four-visit terms through repeated visual demonstration before approving any marked-boundary entry. Oversaw conclusion and required the boundary to remain respected after the fourth visit. Days 321-362 sustained four player strategic priorities while council kept routine work staffed; refused any assumption that the cove is unoccupied or an inland agreement is renewed. Year 2 Days 1-32 guided first-cycle remembrance while maintaining chartered daily autonomy. Approved a reversible nonbinding demonstration in Taluma only, not a renewed inland harvest agreement; encouraged Letha to respect occupied fishing works at Shellbend. Year 2 Day 74: supported Maro/Vessa formal oral chronicle with a distinction between witnessed and reported memories; allowed respectful Shellbend outreach without authorizing fishing rights or a treaty. Year 2 Days 75-119: council balanced workshop and Shellbend diplomacy against winter food/fuel protection; no binding exchange authorized. Acknowledged Nala as first birth recorded by the Circle of Witnesses. Year 2 Day 150: welcomed neighboring craft workers under a public daytime council protocol, with no binding terms; kept minimum survival duties staffed during the winter projects. Year 2 Day 205: approved the safe, recurring Open Learning Days under Vessa, Seli and Maro; kept routine services functioning while project labor rotated. Year 2 Days 206-246: endorsed the hall as a shared voluntary institution and required spring-backup claims to be verified; retains council routine autonomy and guest-boundary restrictions. Year 2 Day 281: hosted first annual Meeting of Many Hands without formalizing a union or treaty; assigned council to keep invitation and hospitality voluntary. Year 2 Days 291-333: supported counted, voluntary witnessed barter custom after two small successful exchanges; reminded council this is neither currency nor a treaty. Year 2 Days 334-Year 3 Day 4: insisted an outpost plan must prove water and flood safety before any settlement decision; authorized only reversible Taluman-ground trade arrangements and voluntary barter. Year 3 Days 5-49: accepted user direction on small voluntary settlement growth, invited visiting households under explicit housing and water limits; welcomed three new residents but reserved large-scale migration/founding for player. Year 3 Day 151: witnessed Anet and Boran voluntarily marry; council maintained consent-based family support. Days 104–164: four separately agreed fish-for-fallen-wood deliveries to Taluma with no boundary crossing or standing trade rights. Year 3 Days 193–217: endorsed inclusive voluntary household traditions and a practical roof-repair celebration, but rejected a premature drive to 100 residents without safe water, housing, food, heating and care. Year 3 Days 230-290: approved separating future family home materials from urgent-repair stocks, prioritizing measured water before major immigration, and host-permitted, nonbinding visits to neighbors. No new territory claimed or treaty signed. Year4 Day175: witnessed birth-record marking and encouraged the practical reading lessons but ruled that the signs must not replace oral history or be treated as absolute proof when symbols are ambiguous. Year4 Day303: agreed that voluntary contacts with a third coastal community remain one-off without treaty; council prioritized players newly chosen records and rain treatment and deferred remote-water search; reminded council the spring remains the binding population limit. Year6 Days41-95: backed fairness-based drought policy and limited experimental catchments without migration until dependable drinking water improves. Year7 Day293: continues council policy of shared water protection, voluntary inter-community learning, safe inland exploration with consent and population expansion constraint. Year7 Day331: endorsed witnessed 18-hearth census confirmed77 residents, instructed health-first allocation and review before any new immigration, recognized adult exploration and voluntary visiting teachers. Year8 Day217: authorized public drought warning when spring fell72 nominal daily shares, coordinated consent-based conditional emergency host inquiries, ensured no coercive relocation. Year9 Days38-125: Delegated trade, safeguarded reserved food and adopted source-specific water management without pretending nonpotable water is potable. Year9 Day299 authorized ten healthy adult Talumans for a one-time escorted geological mission while council kept survival rotations staffed. Year10 Day205: Council approved existing-shelter annex adding only two housing places, explicitly choosing not to invite new residents or use reserved home kits before adequate water is secured. Year11 Day17 convened council when unfamiliar north-coast voyagers asked to join future exchange gatherings; welcomed short respectful visit, deferred any standing access/treaty to next strategic decision. Water audit remains routine, no crisis. Year11: authorized invitation-only market and opted to finish a prepared family house ahead of crowding while keeping freshwater security routine. Year11 Day194 council adopted repeatable invite-confirmed markets and sea-craft exploration while keeping food/family reserves and solved drinking-water infrastructure routine. Year11 Day276 presided over growing invited maritime trading program, green-stone craft apprenticeships and first independent coast trade with all sailors returned; kept freshwater maintenance routine and Northfold OPEN. Year12 Day140: instructed Council to prioritize quality of care and integration, not a compulsory demographic schedule; welcomed two suitably supported skilled adults, updated Year13 exploration readiness charter. Year13 Day47: witnessed completed long voyage and care-first household review; declined rushed growth targets and kept open skilled-family welcome. Year13 Days228-302: endorsed careful new SOUTHERN scouting while keeping family support and village tasks delegated; did not require new housing in uncrowded 106/113 village. Year13 Days303-Year14 Day19 authorized simultaneous permission-first northern and southern reconnaissance and physical hide chart making without neglecting households. Year15 Day55: directed care-conscious defensive readiness with sixteen rotating volunteers and protected village stores without militarizing neighboring contacts. Year15 Days86-125: resolved a conflict over guard duties and household labor by retaining 16 trained volunteers but limiting simultaneous shifts. Asked the council to record disagreement and teach judgment to successors. Year15 Day176: opened a rotating, nonvoting Council Listening Bench so future adult leaders learn how to handle incomplete evidence and real disagreement; supported Seli’s insistence on rotating participants beyond familiar crafts families. No council seat transferred. Year15 Days186-249: led a supervised civic hearing on proposed goodwill replacements; authorized a bounded free-repair expense and an inclusive nonvoting Listening Bench rotation, while preserving seven council seats and household reserves. Year15 Days250-307: expanded the nonvoting civic apprenticeship from council observation to supervised budget/evidence hearings; kept all seven council seats and genuine authority unchanged, asked who would cover the caregiving and boat-repair labor.

named_people.name: Corun
named_people.role: spring tender
named_people.traits: careful observer, concerned about brackish water
named_people.developments: Kept a six-day taste and tide observation. Suspects intrusion into the lower catchment. Wants to separate the upslope trickle from tidal water before it can be trusted. Agreed to continue routine water observations and oversee carried-water delivery to the high-dune residents; did not declare the upper trickle safe as a full settlement water supply. Supervised an upstream draw point and runoff diversion during Days 16-20; observed repeated fresh taste at the upper trickle, but refused to promise dependable winter flow or absolute water safety. Days 36-45 maintained an upper-source observation schedule after light showers; no evidence of major new tidal intrusion at the upper point, but refused to certify long-term water safety. Through Day 55 the guarded upper collection point remained usable for scheduled deliveries; long-term source quality and dry-season capacity remain unknown. Days 56-65 continued daily upkeep and water delivery under permanent council essential-services roster; upper spring remained usable, long-term quality unconfirmed. Days 66-75 kept upper seep collection and water delivery going; new inland stream is observed only, not established as potable supply. Days 76-85 kept protected Taluma spring under routine checks; judged inland stream sight and appearance insufficient to declare it potable. Days 86-95 continued protected spring inspection and daily water-delivery schedule; stressed freezing/storm access risks and that inland stream potability is untested. Day 105: kept upper seep collection usable and maintained deliveries to twelve high-dune residents; no new microbiological or drought/winter guarantee. Day 115: maintained upper spring and carried water to 12 existing high-dune residents, advised that a third shelter needs a sustainable carrying/water-capacity check before occupation. Days 116-125 monitored upper seep and carried water successfully through the squall; spring remained functional but additional household capacity remained unverified. Days 126-135 kept daily flow/delivery checks at the protected upper seep; winter samples met current 67-person needs plus test six-person allotment, but advised a dedicated added carrier and warned seasonal flow/potability still cannot be guaranteed. Days 136-167: continued upper seep observations; seasonal quality uncertain, but provisional six-person surplus remains. Carrier duties prepared for the new empty shelter, not yet expanded in practice. Year 2 Days 214-245: surveyed three Taluma-side wet sites; found a minor western dune trickle after rain but refused to label it independent or drinkable. His clay-lined catchment test cracked; continues daily inspections of the existing upper seep. Year 2 Days 253–274: trialed roof-fed and shallow-dune rainwater collectors; dune lining cracked, roof basin held rain but gathered debris. He prohibited the latter for drinking and continued upper-spring monitoring. Year 2 Days 301-333: led the western exploratory water checks, found the Western Gravel Run, insisted on observing seasonal reliability and rejecting untested drinking-water claims. Year 2 Days 346-359: assessed Western Gravel Run and the higher gravel shelf, observed shrinking dry-weather flow and driftwood flood indicators; refused to certify the site as an independent drinking-water source. Year 3 Days 15-35: surveyed Longbank Terrace as less flood-exposed possible site but refused to certify water as permanent or potable; increased spring monitoring and water carrying for 71 residents. Year 3 Days 63-96: monitored protected main spring through 23 days, improved clean container staging and household water delivery for current village, but refused to count unverified western seeps as safe water. Year 3 Day 211: warned that growing from 73 to 100 requires roughly 37% greater daily safe-water capacity; existing spring supply for such growth is unverified, and outside trickles remain untested for potable use. Year 3 Days 230-290: with apprentices estimated 86-94 average-resident drinking water shares per day over a 12-day drier window, observed low 86; current 73 served, 100 unproven. Spring collection was covered and staged, but this is only one source with potential shared groundwater. Year 3 Days 291-354: documented dry spell spring output dropping as low as 82 resident water-share units/day; with Vessa, rejected one compromised stored-water batch and limited covered container experiments to short same-day use. Still no verified water for 100. Year 4 Day 47: organized repeatable observations and nonintrusive surveys north of Longbank; found Northfold Seep moving after an eleven-day dry spell, but rejected claims of proven safe, independent, year-round drinking supply. Main spring last observed seasonal low remains 82 daily current-person shares. Year 4 Days 63-104: supervised roof-fed nonpotable catchment tests after initial dirty first-rain and leaking open basin. One covered liner collected about 20 large jug loads over three showers; no safe drinking approval or change to spring minimum82. Year4 Days118-175: directed expanded roof rain capture with Arel, two functioning channels and ~18 large-jug covered basin; detected deteriorating batch in third line and isolated it. Record of 72 jugs collected, 54 nonpotably used, 14 lost or discarded, four left covered. Main spring remains only accepted regular potable supply, last observed dry low82 vs current74 people. Marked full/empty record ambiguity corrected. Year4 Days176-240: organized cautious rainwater first-runoff bypass, boiling and clean cooled handling trials, with cracked pottery and one discarded batch; continues to separate provisional treatment from proven safe drinking-source capacity. Year4 Days241-303: tested careful pre-warmed, covered (vented) small-batch rainwater boiling, improved success and measured fuel efficiency; no proof of all-contaminant safety and no spring-flow increase. By player order, suspended remote Northfold/western-water surveys while continuing local spring hygiene and flow monitoring. Year5 Days18-68: supervised daily source-spring monitoring over16 relatively dry days, provisional lowest79 shares/day for74 residents. Directed further first-flush/nonpotable roof catchment and boiling hygiene trials, plus reauthorized non-extractive Northfold observation with no assumption of drinkable water or land rights. Year5 Days69-129: consented two narrow escorted observations at Northfold, learned that source may shrink in summer, proved no extraction permission, and oversaw enlarged nonpotable roof collector plus blocked first-flush response; main spring source low79 shares unchanged. Year5 Days133-194: helped lead small-batch treatment fuel/heat work with experimental losses; efficiency improvements are preliminary and do not establish large-scale safe water. Year5 Days215-280 supervised six household water-treatment trials (48 batches,36 handled successfully,12 discarded). Year5 Day302 final host-approved Northfold warm-season view found negligible surface flow and per player instruction Corun must not revisit or push Northfold without new permission. Year6 Days30-95: wrote spring warning thresholds with individual need protections, still tracks dry observed minimum76 daily shares vs75 residents. Kept nonpotable rain separate from routine source spring. Year6 Day111 introduced family-appropriate public Water Hands rotation with Seli; supervised separate nonpotable collection expansion to116 jugloads, rejected dirty overflow promptly and preserved spring safety. Historical minimum76 for75 residents, no potable capacity claim. Year6 Days258-317: supervised safe local shallow groundwater screening on Taluma land; rejected tide-linked salty coastal seep, guarded inland cloudy slow seep pending dry-season observation, with no potable capacity. Ran storm cistern contamination rejection and kept Northfold strictly closed. Year6 Days334-Year7 Day61: watched landward protected shallow seep through irregular dry period. During 24 nearly rainless days seep diminished but retained isolated damp soil; no tide-linked rise detected, no established yield, safety or independence from existing spring. No deeper digging, withdrawal or new potable tally. NORTHFOLD CLOSED. Year7 Days112-150: supervised stone-ringed, covered shallow well trial away from main spring; observed negligible water ~1.5 jug-loads/12 dry days, excluded from drinking. Begins comparing spring flow and rainy ground while maintaining the Agreement of the Spring. Year7 Day231: compared 26 rain/spring/shallow-shaft observations with Arel and Leni, resisting assumption that rainfall-correlated seep equals independent aquifer; instructed no deeper dig or potable credit. Year7 Day348: wet/dry spring measurements recorded new historical low75 daily resident-equivalent shares for77 people; council activated essential-first drought restrictions; guarded shallow shaft adds zero safe capacity, no Northfold contact. Year8 Day217: observed spring new low72 vs77 nominal resident demand, prioritizing household essential water with nonpotable substitutes for optional work. Oversaw19 short-rotation accepted spring jars, no new source. Year9 Days38-125: Counted 29 rain jug equivalents of discretionary spring withdrawal avoided; kept essential spring-demand concern; one host-approved Northfold observation with no withdrawal. Year9 Days290-347 oversaw nonpotable four-pace enclosed clay conveyance trials; found cleaning hazards and no new potable capacity, sought conditional Northfold and other-neighbor dry-season support. Year10 Day64 authorized nonpotable workshop conduit only and insisted on cleaning, source protection and no claims of newly safe drinking-water supply. Year10 Day219: witnessed nonpotable 24-jug runs delivering23,23,22 and insisted on drain, swab and dry after each shift; still spring low70 for79.

named_people.name: Nemi
named_people.role: fisher and drying-rack steward
named_people.traits: pragmatic, warns that scouting pulls hands away from food collection
named_people.developments: Opposed diverting additional fishers, warning that food reserves remain below target even as wood stores grow. Organized staggered tide-dependent fishing and faster drying/smoking; increased eight-day food output, but warned that winter catch is uncertain. Kept three augmented fishers/preservers on the tidal catch during Days 16-25, adding about fifteen settlement food-days net of immediate consumption accounting, while cautioning that this pace may not last. Days 26-35 maintained fisheries with one supplementary project worker; added eleven food-days gross over ten days but seasonal variability left the settlement one day short of 30-day reserve. Days 36-45 led continued fish and shellfish preserving with four additional workers; net stores improved to 33 days, though seasonal catches remain unreliable. Days 46-55 coordinated four extra fisher-preservers; variable tides yielded 12 settlement-days of preserved food, lifting stores to 35 days. Days 56-65 kept routine fish and shellfish teams working while flexible crews focused inland, preserving nine days of food against ten consumed; food reserve ended at 34 days. Days 66-75 provided practical preservation instruction for an adult apprentice while the routine catch raised food from 34 to 35 settlement-days. Days 76-85 supervised risk-conscious wild seed testing without allowing unproven plants into communal food stores; routine preservation slowed to 9 food-days gross during heavy research allocation. Days 86-95 kept essential fishing and preservation active, adding eleven stored food-days against ten consumed while winter preparations competed for labor. Day 105: led winter fishing with catches periodically weaker in cold rain, preserved 11 settlement-days of food, emphasized that subsistence fishery must not be displaced by unproven farming. Day 115: oversaw improved curing/smoking and added 14 days of food at higher project labor cost, achieving 40-day food winter buffer; warned that stock can fall quickly during storms. Days 116-125 preserved ten days of food in spite of a two-day fishing interruption, but lost one settlement-day equivalent to damp spoilage; urged protection of drying racks. Days 126-135 managed raised, weather-sheltered fish racks, supervised airflow checks, and helped preserve 12 settlement-days food with no measured spoilage this period. Days 188-207: wet weather caused one settlement-day of food spoilage, repaired cover with Arel, maintained safe storage monitoring and supported a modest spring recovery in preserved catch. Days 225-263: 43 food-day equivalents preserved against 39 consumed, but one day equivalent spoiled in damp conditions. She rearranged covered rack rotation, restoring a larger spring food buffer. Days 292-320 authorized four small baskets of preserved fish totaling two settlement-days as agreed exchange, while fishing and drying crews replaced current use and kept food 43 days. Days 321-362 helped preserve forty-eight food-day equivalents in favorable summer conditions, with one day-equivalent spoiled in a damp spell and one offered in modest nonbinding boundary hospitality. Food reserves rose to forty-seven. Year 2 Days 1-32 ordinary crews preserved thirty-eight settlement food-days, with one equivalent used in voluntary craft-visitor hospitality and no land or resource rights granted in exchange. Year 2 Day 74: kept food reserve at 49 days despite one day of hospitality gifts and one of spoilage; limited outside hospitality to affordable stock. Year 2 Days 75-119: food preserved approximately at replacement rate despite autumn weather; one day of fish spoiled during damp spell; held food buffer above thirty-day minimum. Year 2 Days 122-160: directed reversible lagoon tide-guide trials; first surge displaced stones, redesigned version added 2 preserved food-day equivalents to village output. Year 2 Day 205: supervised two reversible local tidal guides; after a surge disrupted one, changed it to be resettable and began releasing juvenile fish during tests. Year 2 Days 206-246: kept fish/shellfish preservation above normal consumption; experimental Taluma lagoon tidal traps monitored, with juvenile-release practice still unproven and one day-equivalent of damp-store loss recorded. Year 2 Days 247–290: coordinated fishing and preservation in time for the annual craft gathering; covered ordinary nutrition and two days-equivalent hospitality, with one rainy spoilage loss. Year 2 Day 362: welcomed a Shellbend fisher rejecting insufficiently dried fish without anger; withdrew suspect provisions and negotiated a fresh voluntary trade later. Year 3 Days 5-49: inspected fish quality at the optional reference-basket trade ground; adjusted preservation labor to food demand from the three new residents. Year 3 Days 104–164: coordinated three Taluman-lagoon reversible tidal trap trials and improved raised fish-drying rack, including replacement after a winter surge. Extra food and spoilage are recorded in 61-day reserves, not added again as free food. Year 3 Days 190–229: taught families how to inspect fish dampness and use raised sheltered drying to prevent waste. Some production benefits from the practices included in the recorded food ledger, not counted again. Year 3 Days 230-290: helped maintain seasonal lagoon fishing and drying stores, keeping 60 days of food by period end while avoiding reliance on the tiny experimental grass plots. Year 4 Day98: safeguarded four food settlement-day equivalents for pregnancy, newborns and carers within general stocks, managed regular dry-food checks to avoid loss and counting twice. Year4 Day167: family caregiving food four-day ringfence remains intact within total66 after rotating older stock, along with daily fish production and preservation. Year4 Days339-350: learned from Reedmouth visiting net craftsperson and conducted cautious two-design float-line trials in Taluma lagoon; food stores remain plentiful but no credited catch uplift from unproven net technology. Year9 Days38-125: Created recurring quality-checked surplus fish exchange with 90-day minimum; completed 10-day barter, accepted Shellbend refusal. Year10 Day117: negotiated five-day food exchange for three consent-offered green stones, keeping ninety-day village floor. Year10 Days175-212: completed ordinary4-day food surplus barter for1 stone load and1 cordage coil, holding90-day trade floor and separate family-care protections. Year11 Day12 hosted witnessed Taluma shore exchange with Reedmouth, Shellbend and Upper Path travelers;8 settlement-food-days bartered for 2 cordage coils, 1 stone load, and two loose green stones available by new Farbank-specific permission; prior90-day trade floor preserved. Year11 Days131-180 organized first repeatable invite-confirmed shore market, accepted7 food-days trade to cordage/stone and separately marketed second green pendant for boat parts; accompanied limited Farbank stone barter Days142-161. Year11 Day232 expanded four-delegation invited market; organized first self-crewed cargo trade at Shellbend Day254 through host permission; kept food above90-day floor and recorded green-stone trade separately from fish. Year13 Day47: voluntary 17-day total preserved food exchange under existing 90-day floor; maintained childcare rations and expedition provisions. Year15 Day55: organized three individually consented trades, bartering thirteen food-days for three cordage coils and two stone loads plus coastal technical knowledge. Year15 Days56-85: initially defended prior repairability claims during Windcut worn-lashing discussion, then accepted Dava’s evidence-based review and authorized a modest goodwill labor exchange, not free concessions or a fixed-price accord. Year15 Days150-169: was frustrated when Dava refused a speculative Reedmouth lashing sale, then publicly endorsed the practice of promising only what testing supports. Piloted voluntary product witness marks rather than claiming a perfect trade standard. Year15 Days186-249: supported Dava’s proposal to replace known failed Windcut binding sets free, despite consuming four valuable cordage coils; distinguished a genuine goodwill gesture from a permanent warranty. Year15 Days250-307: argued that trade credibility also requires practical capacity, not just promising test records; accepted Dava’s capped cordage budget and withheld a new bulk export offer.

named_people.name: Arel
named_people.role: shelter builder
named_people.traits: energetic, believes the camp must move to firmer ground before heavy rain
named_people.developments: Found a rooted dune bench suitable for testing shelters, but insists on confirming a viable water-carrying route before relocating families. Supervised the building of the first six-person high-dune shelter; six people moved in with carried water. Supports further building once water route is dependable. Built the second six-person high-dune shelter with four builders over ten days; all families now have roofed accommodation, though the new bench still depends on carried water. Days 26-30 led a three-person repair crew: reinforced two upper-dune shelters and three old vulnerable roofs, repaired a small seam leak after Day 31 squall. Days 36-45 inspected storm repairs and checked drainage. No new construction; he emphasized that one good squall does not prove winter readiness. Days 56-65 helped build two temporary wooden carrying frames and a small stone-and-clay hearth windbreak; no full-scale road and no measured fuel savings yet. Days 66-75 supervised six paired hearth comparisons. Modest benefit at one prototype in windy weather; recommended replication rather than immediately rebuilding all hearths. Days 76-85 constructed and tested two more simple baffles; one smoked in damp weather. Admitted prototype efficiency is inconsistent, and no village-wide fuel discount is justified. Days 86-95 advised winter roof inspections, noted exact existing shelter capacity and scarce stone stocks; no additional hearth or building construction approved. Day 105: faced criticism for prototypes and repeated comparative hearth trials; favorable cooking tasks used roughly 8-12% less wood, but inconsistent damp-weather smoke and total cost require further work. Day 115: tested three existing hearths in cold/wind; two had 9-11% lower wood use on sheltered cooking tests; stopped using smoky third in gusts. Planned possible 6-place high-dune family shelter, no building started. Days 116-125 managed a swift repair of one roof seam after the squall; continued to withhold new high-dune housing until materials are adequately cured and water delivery is assured. Days 126-135 built the fish-drying cover with Nemi, readied the high-dune housing site without claiming a finished shelter, and limited the smoky hearth to outdoor tests after persistent crosswinds. Day 160: completed the already-authorized additional six-person high-dune shelter, preserving emergency repair stores; hearth trials ongoing with no adopted village-wide savings. Days 168-219: repaired a storm-strained fish storage cover; continued winter/spring cooking trials but refused to certify general hearth fuel savings without safe ventilation and village-wide measurements. Days 225-263: after trials and ventilation adjustments, two prototypes cleared for supervised everyday cooking; documented one actual settlement fuel-day equivalent reduction over last nine days compared with baseline, and kept third smoke-prone unit out of dwellings. Days 321-362 shifted effort from repeating tiny hearth trials to a limited ventilated shared-cooking area using two safe baffle designs. Measured two settlement fuel-day equivalents of total benefit over the 42-day interval. Smoke-prone hearth remains excluded. Year 2 Days 1-32 continued safe shared cooking; measured two baseline fuel-day equivalents saved in 35 days. Offered heat and construction advice for a clay vessel trial, which cracked while drying; no fired pottery success. Year 2 Day 64: supervised low-fire trial with local clay, one settlement fuel-day used beyond ordinary consumption. Two small pots survived cooling, though still not dependable containers. Year 2 Day 94: helped build small pottery drying shed and outdoor firing hollow without consuming scarce stone reserve; supervised fire safety and smoke removal. Hearth savings maintained. Year 2 Day 160: surveyed headland Taluma-local clay/loose stone, improved workshop drying protection, supported fish-trap redesign and continued to count two extra fuel-days for pottery. Year 2 Day 205: supervised safer hauling footholds to the mapped clay-stone source, and two modest pottery firings, keeping the additional fuel cost visible. Year 2 Days 213-239: supervised first common Hall of Many Hands using light pole and cured reed construction; postponed other nonessential structural work and maintained storm repair buffer. Continued safe hearth trials only intermittently. Year 2 Days 254–274: built small stone-edged collectors using limited material stock; accepted failure of dune earthen liner and restricted functional rain basin to nonpotable uses. Year 3 Days 60-82: coordinated two new four-place high-dune shelters using local legal materials and old craft experience; retained repair reserves. No westward outpost. Year 3 Days 165–229: worked with Tama and Boran to double-layer thatch and stop drafts in two high-dune households, checking smoke ventilation. Rejected an overly sealed smoky mock-up, measured marginal fuel savings, and drafted a future housing cost study rather than constructing for 100 prematurely. Year 3 Day 249: joined Sena and Letha on a specifically invited Shellbend home visit. Demonstrated Taluman layered reed roof and smoke-vent design, learned how raised mats and stones under eaves cope with dampness, then piloted a locally adapted reversible repair. Year 4 Day 47: coordinated a phased retrofit across four existing homes; corrected one incorrectly sloped gutter after first rain, preserved smoke vents, and taught apprentices to check repairs by observed weather rather than appearance. Year 4 Days 50-101: adopted witnessed five-part home checks and helped construct two reversible roof-to-basin capture trials; supervised three home retrofits and corrected one wrong-angle drainage outlet before wider adoption. Year4 Days119-169: constructed communal covered rain basin, added and corrected removable roof gutters and learned that one ungraded leak contaminated stagnant water; protected main spring and future house material reserve; taught apprentices runoff inspection and cleaning. Year4 Days176-225: improved runoff handling and raised dry archive shelving; pot heating sometimes failed, and available shelter materials were used without drawing from family-home earmarks. Year6 Days52-78: with Tama designed two sloped stand-alone reed rain catchers, dismantled wind-failed one and reinforced survivor; oversaw24-jug basin and wind-tests. Year6 Days107-143 built and repaired two stand-alone braced rain collectors, recognized one runoff sag failure and provided safe overflow. Three independent collectors operate on Taluma land; no reserved future-home poles/reeds touched. Year6 Days276-301: cover lashing failed in storm but stone-clay large basin body survived; corrected lid and overflow, passed later 35/40-jug severe-weather test. Braced shallow groundwater pits rather than excavating dangerously. Year6 Days326-Year7 Day49: led two storm-braced 24-jug NONPOTABLE rain cistern builds standardized from40-jug design with removable lids, silt bypass, protected overflows. One lid shifted in squall and an initial dirty batch was discarded, repaired, repeated tests passed; new rated capacity204 total but neither potable nor proven for severe drought. Year7 Day139: designed top-braced shallow observation shaft with removable cover and diverted runoff, kept people out of unsupported holes. Recognized that physically diggable well does not imply safe or adequate potable water. Year7 Day226: repaired wind-loosened capped shallow test shaft using spare materials, maintaining safe bracing and spring separation. Year10 Day138: modular cleanout collar design delivered31/32 nonpotable jugs in test, maintenance workload remains heavy. Year10 Day205: used unearmarked materials to add two ventilated sheltered berths to an existing home without extending village water claim. Day219 improved conduit access and slope; still nonpotable. Year15 Days86-125: kept the prepared five-place house kit untouched because five built sleeping spaces remain and no extra household requested immediate separate housing.

named_people.name: Seli
named_people.role: caregiver and Council of the Shore representative
named_people.traits: well-regarded among several households, concerned with vulnerable families
named_people.developments: Joined the seven-member founding council and insisted that the six remaining poorly sheltered inhabitants remain a visible priority. Helped place the last six exposed residents in the second high-dune shelter and asked the council to treat clean water delivery as an ongoing obligation, not a ceremonial construction milestone. Inspected roofs after the Day 31 squall and pressed the council for recurring winter maintenance, particularly for children and older people. Days 36-45 persuaded the council to rotate heavier wood-hauling duties and reserve sheltered space for mending and fiberwork. Days 56-65 pressed for the survival roster to include safe shelter inspections, caregiver cover and rest rotations rather than forcing vulnerable people into heavy work. Days 66-75 supported practical instruction with appropriate expectations for children, while keeping caregivers and shelter inspections staffed. Days 86-95 helped write voluntary family support plan for winter health, maternal care, childcare and future shelter/water needs; no pregnancy or birth assumed. Day 105: organized voluntary conversations with prospective parents and two experienced caregivers for maternal/infant support, childcare, nutrition and housing needs; no pregnancy or birth reported. Day 115: consulted households about voluntary new family housing and helped choose near-existing-carry-route shelter site; caregiver mentoring continues, no pregnancy or birth inferred. Days 116-125 checked that displaced households were not created by the squall, maintained the voluntary family-care program, and advocated preparing spare shelter without overusing emergency repair materials. Days 126-135 maintained voluntary family planning and caregiving while defending the emergency material reserve until spare housing can be safely built. Day 160: spare housing for six now exists, supporting voluntary future household growth without any new births or assumed pregnancies. Days 168-219: continued voluntary infant and family-care teaching, supporting households planning growth; no new births or confirmed pregnancies were added. Days 225-263: helped existing adults Rema and Jorin establish a household in an already completed high-dune shelter. Rema privately reported signs of an expected first child; Seli offers voluntary support without assuming a guaranteed pregnancy or birth. Day 320 continued voluntary support for Rema and Jorin; no conclusion about pregnancy or birth can yet be drawn. Days 321-362 continued voluntary and private care for Rema, whose physical signs have become more consistent with pregnancy but remain without modern diagnostic certainty. No baby counted, no birth assumed. Year 2 Days 1-32 continued private voluntary care and nutrition for Rema. Physical signs remain increasingly consistent with pregnancy but no birth, exact dates or guaranteed outcomes are asserted. Year 2 Day 74: continued confidential voluntary support to Rema; pregnancy appears increasingly probable but birth remains in future and uncertain. Year 2 Day 116: assisted Rema in childbirth alongside two experienced carers. Both Rema and daughter Nala alive and resting by Day 119; voluntary family-care program continues. Year 2 Day 160: continued voluntary infant-care instruction and support for Rema and infant Nala; no change in household size. Year 2 Day 205: continues caring for Rema and infant Nala, sets age and safety limits for learning sessions, ensuring children are never used to replace adult workers. Year 3 Days 5-49: continued voluntary maternal and family care and interviewed willing new residents regarding housing, water and child welfare before council admission. Year 3 Days 65-103: organized voluntary newborn/parent care exchanges, shelter hearth clearances and support for couples hoping to raise children. No public claims about private pregnancies or guaranteed birth. Year 3 Days 104–164: facilitated optional adult introductions, witnessed Anet and Boran freely marrying Day 151, and offered noncoercive pregnancy, early childhood, family and caregiving support. No births or confirmed pregnancies recorded. Year 3 Days 165–229: helped establish optional seasonal household support rituals, caregiving circles and the Night of Shared Fires; welcomes all household types and teaches safe pregnancy and infant care without coercion. No new birth or confirmed pregnancy. Year 3 Day 282: Anet privately reported signs of a possible early pregnancy; Seli offered confidential voluntary care and practical advice. Nothing confirmed and no birth is counted. Year 4 Day 47: supports Anet’s continuing pregnancy and voluntary family/household wellbeing; continues keeping new family privacy and recognizes no births during this turn. Year 4 Day98: co-established the needs-based family provisioning reserve with Nemi; Anet receiving continuing pregnancy support, no birth yet. Year4 Day167: cared for Anet during delivery of daughter Tavi; both stable, followed with voluntary maternal and newborn support, food reserve rotated/replenished and household mats checked. All child care is consensual and needs-based. Year4 Days176-240: oversaw safe water-handling comparisons and ordinary infant care; Anet and Tavi remained well. No new births observed. Year4 Days241-303: maintained infant care and household support; joined monitoring of clean-water transfer to prevent used utensils recontaminating boiled batches; no births or deaths occurred. Year5 Days19-61: monitored clean-covered prompt-use boiled rainwater trials, rejected dirty or doubtful batches, kept spring water prioritized for households and children; no generalized drinkable certification. Year5 Days69-129: maintained care support with 4 reserved food-days; watched infant Tavi and toddler Nala with caregivers; supervised prompt use of a few correctly heated water batches, without certifying long storage. Year6 Day47: challenged an unfair equal-household allocation plan; designed essential-care exceptions and witnessed appeal procedures for drought water. Year6 Day91: corrected mistaken count after family challenge. Year6 Day132 upheld equal-value caregiving and light record work for households unable to do heavy gutter/roof tasks, ensuring water access is not tied to labor and protecting vulnerable families. Year7 Day38: helped Anet during birth of Ona. Coordinated water priorities for infant care as village headcount reached77, above spring historical low76 daily shares. Year7 Day331 census protected confidential family-care details; ensured twin-hearth child counted once and water allocations recognized care, without coercion or exclusion. Year8 Day162: designed family-first emergency water and sanitation plan, prevented assumptions that brief jar trials establish long-term potability. Year9 Days38-125: Protected potable/hygiene boundaries while optional craft work used coastal/rain water; household care never contingent on trade/work. Year10 Day205: inspected two-berth addition for ventilation and caregivers; safe sleeping improvement not proof of increased drinking water. Day219 forbade linking experimental conduit to spring-water households. Year13 Day9: attended Aven birth and maintained childcare/elder relief program; safe care remained part of council routine. Year14 Day326 supported Tira and newborn Oli; adjusted household coverage so Hadan could assist family. Year15 Day177: objected to limiting future civic training to the traders’ and teachers’ own circles; Esha agreed to rotate Listening Bench participation across adult households. Year15 Days250-307: required leadership apprentices to account for real household-care hours and safeguarded protected provisions during optional fiber experimentation.

named_people.name: Tovan
named_people.role: experienced wood gatherer
named_people.traits: favors careful harvesting of fallen deadwood, wary of wasting time on exhausted gathering sites
named_people.developments: Days 26-35 guided gatherers along longer wooded-dune routes and identified usable dead timber without cutting living trees, helping council reach a 31-day fuel reserve. Days 36-45 kept fuel stores level by bringing wood from farther along established routes; warned that transporting deadwood now costs as much effort as finding it. Days 46-52 led four-person inland reconnaissance to a more heavily wooded swale, marked foot route, and observed weathered tool-like scars on a dead trunk. Returned without injury, but warns that hauling wet or heavy logs one day across dunes may defeat any supposed gain. Days 56-65 tested the cleared route and two hand frames; a small relay delivered only one day of additional firewood, while a follow-up inspection of old woodworking scars yielded stone flakes but no sign of a current neighboring settlement. Cautioned against treating unknown woodland as common property. Days 66-72 led four scouts past the wooded swale to a stony stream, finding a small cold-ash stone setting and possible track; he urged caution before new harvesting or assumption of unused land. Days 76-81 led peaceful return to stream; observed two adults across water, chose not to approach or presume their intentions, and reported short stream-flow observations. Days 86-92 led four unarmed envoys to the inland stream; established tentative reciprocal goodwill by offering a few dried fish and accepting a woven fiber loop, with both parties remaining on their own banks. He declined to treat gestures as shared language or permission to take timber. Day 105: supported fuel gathering on existing authorized routes, warned against overworking increasingly distant hauling crews and asked for cost accounting of hearth conversion. Day 115: coordinated harder longer hauling to bring back 15 days wood fuel, achieving 39 stored days after 10 burnt; cautioned that one more day and continued maintenance still needed. Days 116-125 managed distant wood gathering of eleven fuel-days while retaining rest rotations; the 40-day fuel buffer was reached but harvesting remains laborious. Days 126-135 trialed a braced carrying frame on the known woodland corridor, returned one fuel-day on a short relay, and reported muddy sections requiring caution. Day 167: noticed three visitors arrive along the inland way, including a red-ochre wristband resembling that from first contact; advised cautious reception and no assumed territorial rights. Day 167 accompanied Esha for peaceful boundary reception; exchanged modest gifts and noted an uninterpreted palm gesture about the wooded swale. Day 219: found new ochre cord stretched between stones across the familiar wooded route, with two people watching on the far side. Kept his party short of the markers and halted disputed gathering pending council and guiding-intelligence decisions. Days 225-263: respected the ochre-marked inland exclusion and relied on safer coastal/fringe deadwood; 35 settlement fuel-day equivalents gathered but replacement lagged demand, exposing risk of reserve decline. Days 264-291: led three safe, boundary-side meetings. Demonstrated deadwood-only collecting with short branches, illustrated modest repeat trips using pebbles, respected all ochre markers; reported that proposed access is a possibility, not a confirmed permission. Continued warning council of fuel deficit. Days 298,305,312,319 guided hauling parties on escort-approved narrow route; brought 9 food-day-equivalent fuel loads back across four controlled collections. Warned that a successful pilot is not a permanent supply. Days 321-362 made three peaceful ochre-line meetings with Vessa; no crossing, reentry or new binding bargain. Supported legal local wood collection while fuel stock declined slightly. Year 2 Day 150: helped invite an inland craftsperson without crossing ochre boundaries; winter fuel gathering remained on approved local coast/fringe only. Year 2 Day 205: maintains fuel on permitted coastal routes while a clay/stone haul path is improved; the inland ochre boundary remains untouched. Year 2 Days 206-246: coordinated legal coast-fringe fuel gathering as construction displaced some project labor. Firewood reserve now 32 days, nearing standing minimum despite safe hearth savings; ochre-boundary restriction honored. Year 2 Days 247–290: refocused existing legal coastal wood crews and permitted hauling to rebuild reserves from 32 to 34 days while optional projects continued; inland cord boundary honored. Year 2 Days 346-359: helped survey the westward walking route and flood-high vegetation, noted distance of hauled shelter supplies; maintained legal fuel routes and did not cross ochre boundary. Year13 Days15-38: voyaged as shore scout and safety observer, identified new inlet weir patterns while avoiding unknown uninvited shore. Year13 Days252-270: led first SOUTHERN exploratory reach beyond Shellbend with Rela and Mata; saw Windcut Bay from offshore, did not claim inhabited shores, returned Tidefin safely. Year13 Days316-332 met invited Windcut fisher Vara through gestures; Year13 Days358-Year14 Day6 charted offshore White-Reed Point southward, no assumed access, both missions returned. Year14 Days205-224: led consented inland route visit with Ilan, Kelan and one adult trainee to High-Shelf Rest; returned safely. Year14 Days261-342 expanded twelve-person voluntary Shore Watch training; investigated damaged Windcut fishing stakes without blaming people and joined the permitted Windgrass Hollow outing. Year15 Day55: co-trained sixteen Shore Watch volunteers with Kelan and confirmed separate guest and emergency responses in a low-visibility shoreline event. Year15 Days86-125: adjusted Shore Watch rota to keep watch and greeting roles clearly distinct, after training competed with essential work.

named_people.name: Vessa
named_people.role: elder fiberworker and cordage teacher
named_people.traits: meticulous, dislikes poorly dried fibers and hasty workmanship
named_people.developments: Days 36-45 guided two adult project workers using older cured plant fibers to make two sound cordage coils; warned against consuming the still-drying reed stock. Days 66-75 began regular voluntary cordage lessons with an adult learner; one cured reed/rush bundle became one usable cordage coil, but proper quality control remains important. Days 76-85 continued instruction and co-produced one sound cordage coil using one cured reed bundle, while encouraging learners to recognize poor work before it fails. Day 105: selected by households for a winter council seat after an unnamed delegate voluntarily stood aside; now represents crafts and education while retaining voluntary apprenticeships. Day 115: examined whether reed stock was sufficiently dried to build roofs and cautioned against using wet bundles in a prospective shelter. Days 126-135 inspected the cured reed stock; 17 bundles are roof-grade and 3 newly gathered still damp after food-cover work. Worked with Nemi to keep cover breathable and avoid trapped moisture. Days 168-219: supervised another usable cordage coil from one cured plant-fiber bundle and continued rotating apprentices without displacing essential work. Days 225-263: recognized Iren as ready to make ordinary cordage independently after several successful samples; kept mentorship for critical loads and continued voluntary teaching. Days 264-291: used woven loop and visual demonstrations to build practical trust and make limited object-based communication possible; warned that concrete language and amounts are still uncertain. Day 295 used four stones, fish baskets and living-versus-fallen wood demonstration to verify mutual comprehension; witnessed confirmations and separate assent before each visit, though language remains rudimentary. Days 321-362 practiced repeating fish and flowing-water gestures at three nonbinding visits. The spoken term aru was heard again but remains untranslated; observed a hard-fired-looking inland vessel, origin uncertain. Supervised two sound cordage coils with Iren. Year 2 Days 13-20 welcomed two willing inland craft visitors at Taluma and demonstrated fiberwork with Iren. Saw clay mixed with crushed temper and attempted a Taluman vessel, which cracked while drying. Continued noting gestures without claiming fluency. Year 2 Day 74: led clay temper and drying experiments with Iren, yielding two small intact low-fired but porous trial vessels; co-founded Circle of Witnesses to transmit reliable oral history. Year 2 Day 94: opened small weather-sheltered, ventilated pottery preparation/drying space and outdoor firing hollow; taught two apprentices, five of nine new fired pieces survived, two held water overnight. Still not sealed bulk vessels. Year 2 Day 150: hosted one inland clay worker and one coastal fisher for voluntary skill sharing, helping pupils compare temper, weights and cordage; fired 6 intact of 11 trial vessels. Year 2 Day 205: hosted two voluntary small craft gatherings and helped launch Open Learning Days with knot and clay-shaping demonstrations. Four of ten new fired vessels held water overnight. Year 2 Days 239-244: organized cross-household learning in the new Hall of Many Hands and hosted separate willing visitors from Shellbend and inland, teaching basic fiber and ceramic skills without assuming a language treaty. Year 2 Day 281: led first annual gathering of inland and Shellbend craftspeople at the Hall of Many Hands, supervising voluntary demonstrations and exchange of techniques. Year 2 Days 305-328: helped visitors and apprentices demonstrate reciprocal pebble counts and goods inspection; observed a one-off fiber-for-ochre exchange at the Taluma side of the marked woodland boundary. Year 2 Day 353: helped prepare removable trade mats and showed learners how to assess cordage quality; advised visitors may refuse goods or leave freely. Year 3 Days 5-49: worked with Iren to improve fitted pottery lids for dry seed storage, while teaching children that repeated trials include failures; welcomed new Shellbend toolmaker Daro as potential teacher. Year 3 Days 252-290: taught younger craftspeople how to copy a raised woven mat and evaluate small replaceable reed wall panels; kept brief records through demonstrations and oral chronicle, no writing assumed. Year 3 Days 291-354: hosted consenting Shellbend and inland guest builders and ran careful short-term covered water-vessel trials. Organized safe youth demonstrations separate from adults’ escorted expeditions. Year 4 Day 24: joined Maro in designing voluntary specialization by observed practice and oral witnessing, safeguarding older children from hazardous work and converting neighbor exchanges into teachable local skills. Year 4 Days 76-107: mentored apprentices in copying standardized simple clay/wood marks for roof, rainfall, jug quantities and season observations, while pottery fuel remained limited. Year4 Days125-172: standardized a small learned sign inventory with Leni and Maro; supervised copying/interpretation and limited low-fired record tablet tests with clay costs. Warning: symbols do not encode speech; a reader can infer a narrow practical message only. Year4 Day225: standardized shape of practical marks and helped fire nine durable exemplar tablets for permanent Hall archive; declines to call the system complete writing. Year4 Days241-303: coached careful pottery shaping for lower-crack boiling vessels, and archive tiles with clearly differentiated person and household marks; still insists script does not record phonetic names. Year4 Days339-341: taught Taluman pottery and roof knowledge to two visiting Reedmouth artisans at Hall, accepted demonstration of bone-awl piercing and net floats; facilitated apprentices with safe practice. Year5 Days69-129: demonstrated Taluman layered drainage and administrative tally marks to invited Reedmouth teachers while helping test water-collector lids; kept limited fuel costs in workshop. Year5 Days133-194: helped lead small-batch treatment fuel/heat work with experimental losses; efficiency improvements are preliminary and do not establish large-scale safe water. Year7 Days16-20: voluntary Hall of Many Hands exchange includes visiting Reedmouth and Shellbend children with caregivers and an inland fiberworker, credited source skills in witnessed records. Year7 Day243: credited willing Upper Path stoneworker for stone-flaking demonstrations, with no source-location claim. Year8 Day209: hosted Upper Path runoff and natural settling instruction, credited guest and warned apprentices that clear-looking water need not be safe. Year9 Day325 examined host-approved riverworn green comparison pebble; no firm mineral ID or original outcrop established. Year10 Day26 compared three separately documented green-stone samples, observed visible resemblance but no mineral species proof or original artifact provenance. Year10 Days171-212: taught Daro reversible cord sleeve and patient abrasive finishing; observed six-stone provenance and rejected a quick destructive drilling trial. Year11 Days208-276 co-taught two learners safe abrasive polishing, removable lashings and not wasting rare green stone. Year14 Day19 supervised preparation and marking of three purchased dressed animal hides for the growing cartography practice. Year15 Day55: tested Windcut replaceable fishing-stake lashings and supervised source-credit voluntary craft teaching. Year15 Days56-85: helped examine fiber abrasion and set two repairable lashing variants for fair comparison under Windcut host observation. Year15 Day147: recognized reinforced binding cost more fiber and survived only short Windcut trials, declining to pronounce season-long durability without further testing. Year15 Days186-249: improved replaceable binding design with reed wear sleeves while warning that no full storm-season test exists; allocated craft labor away from commercial production. Year15 Days250-307: supervised several braided and conventional binding tests; documented premature wetting loosening in first trial and refused any blanket claim of durability.

named_people.name: Iren
named_people.role: adult fiberwork apprentice
named_people.traits: careful and deliberate, counts twists and knots to avoid weak cords
named_people.developments: Joined Vessa’s first formal ten-day volunteer learning rotation and helped finish a sound coil of cordage; still needs supervision. Year 2 Day 17 taught a visiting inland craftsperson basic Taluman fiber splicing under Vessa's supervision; completed another sound cordage coil in ordinary work. Year 2 Day 205: demonstrates practical cord repair to willing older learners and helps Vessa form pots; no instant mastery among pupils. Year 2 Day 325: prepared a sound cordage coil through adult fiberwork and demonstrated fair counted exchange with inland visitors on the Taluman side of the ochre marker. Year 3 Days 20-44: tested fourteen small pottery forms with Vessa; eight survived, three lid pairs useful in short sheltered dry-storage tests. Year 4 Day 47: shaped a repeatable small lidded dry-storage vessel under Vessa; still requires help controlling firing heat and has not proved long-term storage. Year5 Days133-194: helped lead small-batch treatment fuel/heat work with experimental losses; efficiency improvements are preliminary and do not establish large-scale safe water. Year8 Day193: led 24 trial vessels with Vessa, 15 firing survivors,11 passed supervised short lid/handling checks; workshop now active. Year10 Day48 fired six socketed clay conduit sleeves for twelve-pace enclosed nonpotable experiment and identified one cracked sleeve; cleaning practicality remains a barrier. Year10 Day219: fitted replaceable conduit collars and quick-lift access points; after a three-day stagnant test discovered persistent seam film, so nonpotable-only precautions continue.

named_people.name: Dava
named_people.role: adult food-preservation apprentice
named_people.traits: curious, notices how weather affects drying
named_people.developments: Joined Nemi’s first formal teaching rotation to learn cleaning, smoke-drying and storage checks at existing fish racks; still needs supervision. Year 4 Day 47: demonstrated sorting and inspecting cured fish to new adult learners, remaining under Nemi for major storage decisions. Year15 Days56-85: challenged Nemi to separate a brief Taluman bench test from gritty Windcut tidal performance. Earned greater responsibility for checking claims made about exported techniques. Year15 Day160: held firm against offering a season-long binding guarantee without evidence, costing an immediate possible transaction but earning Nemi’s explicit trust. Became a founding nonvoting Council Listening Bench observer. Year15 Days186-249: presented replacement-cost evidence at Council Listening Bench and traveled with Sena and pilot Rela to deliver four free reinforced repair sets to Windcut; began documenting scope and uncertainty in Three Witness Marks. Year15 Days250-307: with Iset presented competing cordage proposals, limited test spending to five coils while protecting service repairs, and declined claims of export-quality durability; began learning to trade off immediate craft production against experimental evidence.

named_people.name: Sora
named_people.role: coastal wild-plant gatherer and cultivation experimenter
named_people.traits: patient observer who distinguishes edible seedheads from unknown plants and records where they grow
named_people.developments: During Days 76-85 compared local wild-grass seedheads with Nemi and another worker, prepared two tiny sowing trials close to Taluma away from seep protection, without using the protected seed reserve. No germination or yield yet. Days 86-95 observed a few apparent seedlings in one protected wild-grass trial and none in the other. Prepared tentative planting observations for spring, with no crop yield or protected seed use. Day 105: monitored first small wild-grass trial through early winter; a few shoots survived, others yellowed and second sandy plot did not germinate convincingly. No harvest, reliable growing season or seed-stock usage. Days 208-219: some of the protected winter wild-grass sprouts strengthen in warmer weather; selected a comparative spring observation patch using locally gathered seeds without drawing down protected seed or attributing harvest. Days 225-263: observed first tiny seedheads on overwintered sheltered wild-grass plants. Collected a small observational sample, not edible grain in stores; tests spring sowing and seasonal contrasts. Days 321-362 prepared three roughly 10x15-pace wild-grass trial beds and a comparison patch with seed gathered locally. Mulched ground gave uneven early emergence; dry sandy patch less successful. No harvest credited and protected seeds untouched. Year 2 Days 1-32 saved a small dry seed sample from the old patch, too little to feed anyone, and compared the increasingly distinct three larger trial beds. Protected seed reserve untouched. Year 2 Day 74: compared trial beds and retained modest viable selected seed from mulched soil, not counted as stored food. Sandy plot mostly unsuccessful. Year 2 Day 205: keeps second-generation trial seeds and winter field observations, inviting safe participation in soil comparisons but recording no food-scale harvest. Year 2 Days 232-246: continued small second-generation wild-grass spring beds, recording sprouts and losses; no food-scale harvest and protected emergency seed untouched. Year 2 Days 247–290: followed next-generation wild-grass trial plots through spring, noting stronger growth in mulched soil; still no settlement-scale harvest and protected seed untouched. Year 3 Day 4: continuing small successor-grass cultivation trials; observing seed quality and moisture. No food-scale cultivation yield credited. Year6 Days96-169: coordinated a 24x40 pace common cultivated wild-grass field with 6 rotating adults, mature older plots contributed 2 whole-settlement food-days; new sown rows only emerged unevenly, protected seed2 untouched. Year6 Day236: first mature grain from enlarged common wild-grass field (3 settlement-food-days), compared24 nonpotable jugs on two strips against unwatered controls. Started annual shared planting and small harvest custom, protecting seed. Year6 Days281-317: compared24 plump-headed experimental grass seeds vs24 small-headed comparison, 17 vs11 germinated, began next small field strips; no new mature crop-scale harvest, protected survival seed2 untouched. Year6 Days318-Year7 Day68: carefully repeated 24-vs24 selected wild-grass seed trial through maturity;12 of17 germinated selected seedlings and8 of11 comparison reached harvest, producing21 vs14 standard seed-head bundles in matched small plots. New common cultivation yields five edible village-food-day equivalents after planting seed saved; older beds yield two, together seven included in food production, fishing still dominant. Year7 Day172: repeated full-season selected vs control96 seeds each; germination74vs69, mature51vs49, 78vs71 standardized seedheads. Eight edible common-field food days plus2 older plots within production; bird losses noted; selected reserve and emergency seed preserved. Year7 Day282: completed fourth-generation selected-control144/144 comparison through mature harvest. Some seed-head improvement (148vs129 units), but wind damage/soil confounds; 12 cultivated food-day equivalents within production118. Year7 Days316-355: planted128 selected seeds in windbreak strips and128 selected in unsheltered comparison;97vs95 germination,82vs67 still standing after wind, repeated observation planned; no full yield yet. Three old-bed food-days within69 total output. Year8 Day238: harvested windbreak+mulch,windbreak,exposed+mulch 64-seed plots with36/33/29 mature plants and66/57/49 head units; protected selected and emergency seed. Year9 Days38-125: Maintained control strips and seed protection; small existing mature beds provided five food-day equivalents already included in produced total. Year9 Days282-347 produced eight food-day equivalents from mature experimental and older grain beds despite postponed further field enlargement while 10 adults explored inland. Year9 late summer to Year10 early autumn: nine food-days of cultivated grain from established managed plots included within general food production; seed reserve protected; held back on enlarging plots until water and soil results clearer.

named_people.name: Maro
named_people.role: Household delegate, Council of the Shore winter session
named_people.traits: practical representative of family needs; favors accountable labor and supply decisions
named_people.developments: Previously one of two unnamed household delegates; identity recorded as Maro during Day 105 seasonal review. Retained a council seat while the other unnamed delegate voluntarily yielded their seat to Vessa. No authority beyond the existing Council charter. Day 115: supported emergency repair stockpile threshold before any optional dwelling project to avoid making all families vulnerable to roof damage. Year 2 Day 71: helped institute Circle of Witnesses and a simple lunar/tidal counting aid; insisted contradictory recollections be preserved as distinct rather than invented as common fact. Year 2 Day 116: Circle of Witnesses added birth of Nala to the oral chronicle as an eyewitness-supported event, with testimony from Seli and parents. Year 2 Day 153: Circle of Witnesses recorded the gathering as eyewitness testimony while leaving the identity of coastal visitors and inland craft workers uncertain. Year 2 Day 205: Circle of Witnesses integrates oral histories and moon/tide marks into Open Learning Days, retaining eyewitness/secondhand distinctions. Year 2 Day 242: helped the Circle of Witnesses open the Hall of Many Hands with oral accounts of Nala’s birth, the first winter storm, and the coastal contacts; maintained competing versions where memories differed. Year 2 Day 281: gave the gathering an oral place in the Circle of Witnesses, distinguishing observed skills from uncertain words and stories. Year 2 Day 323: recorded simple stone-counted barter demonstrations in the Circle of Witnesses and taught that each side may refuse an exchange, without calling it an enforced agreement. Year 2 Day 353-Year 3 Day 2: facilitated a trading ground with visible counts and voluntary witnesses, learning that a counted basket is not necessarily a good-quality basket; taught quality inspection alongside arithmetic. Year 3 Days 5-49: developed optional reference-basket volume and visible goods-inspection practices after an exchange temporarily stalled on unequal measures; emphasized ability to refuse. Year 3 Days 104–164: recorded Anet and Boran's voluntary marriage in the oral chronicle and practiced visible inspection and counted barter at the four winter fuel exchanges. Year 3 Days 193–229: documented first Roof-Raising Day and Night of Shared Fires, recording which roof methods succeeded and which leaked or smoked, so rituals preserve practical evidence alongside memory. Year 3 Days 249-290: documented two reciprocal, one-time house-building visits, taught older learners to separate observation from assumptions, and recorded two new reserve categories: earmarked for families and essential storm repairs. Year 4 Day 24: introduced witnessed oral accounts of demonstrable apprenticeship skill in Hall of Many Hands; pupils show results to mentors, with no claim of invented writing or fixed schooling. Year 4 Days 76-107: linked Circle of Witnesses oral memories with small conventional durable quantities-and-object signs for water records. Complex histories remain orally corroborated; no phonetic script yet. Year4 Days125-175: guided first standardized practical account signs beyond pure tallies, with apprentice-reader verification. Discovered ambiguous full/empty jug record and revised syntax with explicit marks. Kept birth of Tavi in witnessed oral chronicle, linked with a concise nonphonetic household/child clay token; no full writing system yet. Year4 Day225: became founding curator of Hall archive; new marks and witnessed family and inventory records are copied alongside oral accounts; five damp tablet losses motivated protections. Year4 Days260-298: guided six household relationship tablets and oral witnesses; taught second reader to flag contradictory person tokens. One reused sign was discovered and corrected, preventing erroneous kinship records. Year5 Day3: oversaw witness-checked pictographic coastal travel marks for tide hazard, visited settlement and unverified smoke observations, storing records at the Hall. History remains oral in substance. Year5 Days24-68: recorded high/low tide observations and uncertain surge warnings in witness-backed simple pictograms; maintained archive of rain jug and spring readings without claiming written speech or perfect forecasting. Year5 Days69-129: witnessed the nonbinding Reedmouth seasonal visit invitation pictogram and recorded Northfold consent boundaries in both short proto-writing and oral chronicle. Year5 Day171-172: helped with the voluntary shared coastal craft-learning sessions at the Hall. Year5 Days271-282 verified community origin of techniques with oral witnesses and seven fired/non-fonetic credit plaques at annual Meeting of Many Hands; corrected Reedmouth tide-warning misattribution. Year6 Days41-95: recorded Agreement of the Spring in witnessed pictographic water-share marks; organized translation of household requests and correction appeals with oral testimony. Year7 Day274: recorded Upper Path teaching sources, initial inland waypoints and seasonal crop comparison with oral witnesses in Hall archive. Year7 Day331: led full witnessed household census, found a child wrongly repeated in two hearth-care records, reconciled 18 hearth groups8x5+7x4+3x3=77, persons44 adults26 children7 elders; visiting learners and guides excluded. Archived non-sensitive summaries. Year8 Day162: prepared witnessed privacy-respecting 18-hearth emergency care roster and teacher credit tablets for Upper Path runoff lesson. Year9 Days38-125: Witnessed independent trade and water-source markings with household records, teaching value without guaranteeing exchange terms. Year10 Day190: led first complete witnessed household recount since Year7, 79 permanent residents in18 hearths, with Y9 newborn Dena and Y10 newborn Oru each counted once; outsiders excluded.
